subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO MAKE GOVERNMENT DEFICIT SPENDING ILLEGAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask, with the unanimous consent of the House, for permission to propose a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. Given the crippling effect our inflation rate has on Canadians by reason of the fact that it erodes their real purchasing power, and the fact that most economists including John Kenneth Galbraith, philosopher-king to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recognize that excessive government spending is a major cause of inflation, I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That this House instruct the government to introduce legislation to make government deficit spending illegal.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of State (Fisheries) whether he can report to the House on the outcome of the recent ICNAF meeting in Montreal and, more specifically, whether he can tell the House what new role was discussed for Canada through its membership in ICNAF after our unilateral declaration comes into effect on January 1?

subtopic: ROLES OF CANADA IN ICNAF AFTER EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE 200 MILES-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not yet been briefed in detail on the latest development as I have just returned to Ottawa within the last half-hour. speechtext:

the acquisition of new equipment, and the new role proposed for the armed forces in this regard?

maintopic: MEASURES FOR SURVEILLANCE OF 200-MILE FISHING ZONE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said in Montreal, and I say here, that we are doubling the level of boardings and inspections this year, which will mean about 1,200. REASON FOR ABOLITION OF SPECIAL INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: DIVISION-SUGGESTED DISCLOSURE OF MATTERS UNDER INVESTIGATION AT TIME DIVISION DISBANDED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration arising from the abolition of the special investigation division of the Unemployment Insurance Commission within the last year, at a time when the need for such a division seemed to be clearly demonstrated. Will the minister tell the House why the special investigation division of the UIC was abolished and the reasons some of its members were then sent to far distant points in the UIC system after abolition took place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: REASON FOR ABOLITION OF SPECIAL INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: DIVISION-SUGGESTED DISCLOSURE OF MATTERS UNDER INVESTIGATION AT TIME DIVISION DISBANDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I most certainly will. The special investigation division existed, and it was found that there was a very considerable overlap between its function and the function of the benefit control operation. After considerable analysis and discussion, including some discussions with me, we decided to make the change.
The special investigation division was also very centralized here in Ottawa, and the cases to which we wanted attention paid were obviously very often in the regions. It was a very logical organizational decision made in March of 1975 to integrate the SID into the regional benefit control operation.
On the second part of the hon. member's question, I would have to check the details, but I presume that since we did want to decentralize and get the investigation where the action is, as it were, some people were transferred in order to make it more efficient.

subtopic: REASON FOR ABOLITION OF SPECIAL INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: DIVISION-SUGGESTED DISCLOSURE OF MATTERS UNDER INVESTIGATION AT TIME DIVISION DISBANDED
speechtext: Having been forewarned that the minister would use decentralization as the reason, I will ask him this: Specifically will the minister agree to make public all matters which the special investigation division had under scrutiny at the time of its abolition, and if he will not agree, why will he not agree?

subtopic: REASON FOR ABOLITION OF SPECIAL INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: DIVISION-SUGGESTED DISCLOSURE OF MATTERS UNDER INVESTIGATION AT TIME DIVISION DISBANDED

The House resumed, from Thursday, June 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, at one o'clock, I was speaking about the O'Donnell case in Toronto where a man had killed a young school teacher, going across the Don in Toronto, by hitting her with a stone, raping her and then dragging her out of the Don Valley. A few days later he was picked up by the police for the murder he had committed on a defenceless young school teacher who had no chance of saying a word to defend herself or to prepare for the next world.
There was also the case of a young sex offender who was released from penitientiary because the psychiatrist said he was unlikely to kill again, but within two years he had killed five young men in Quebec City. Just a couple of years ago, a 26-year old female was taken by an intruder who had entered her locked apartment by using a master key. She and her husband had been awakened by the noise, and in their night-clothes had gone to see what was happening.
The husband was warned not to call the police or his wife would die. The wife was taken by the intruder at knife point. He drove her around Toronto for nearly five hours, then raped her, subjected her to all types of sexual aberrations, and when she was not complying, the ever-ready knife was poised. The criminal in this case was a 19-year old youth who had been in psychiatric care from the age of five. He had recently been released from the hospital for the criminally insane at Penetanguishene, Ontario. This young woman is still not working. She cannot work. She is still suffering from the ravages of that night and the indelible imprint the tragedy made on her. She will probably go through life suffering, as a result.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: They should hang the psychiatrist.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
You have an idea. At least you are in favour of capital punishment. These are the responsibilities, Mr. Speaker. Then there is the little girl of ten years of age who just a couple of weeks ago was raped and had her

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
skull blown to pieces. That little, innocent girl never had her day in court or a chance to repent.
Mr. Speaker, I say to you that these are our responsibilities to keep law and order in society. That is why we have police forces. That is why social workers and all our levels of courts are needed, to try to see that justice is carried out on this earth. I have tried to point out that in no way can I watch prisoners sentenced to 15 years or longer walk up those corridors day after day, with bars on the windows and doors bolted. It is dying daily, inch by inch. The chance of rehabilitation goes out the door as the never-ending days pass. Is this what we really want-the torture, the wasting of the mind, the cruelty of long years of suffering?
I have heard people say they are abolitionist because they want to make the criminal live and, day after day, relive and suffer through a long prison sentence. Over and over again I have heard the relatives of a critically ill patient say it was nice to see him, or her, die so quickly and not suffer through a long, agonizing and lingering illness. What is one's philosophy as an abolitionist? The ultimate in cruelty is not the humane way. You can let a man leave this world quietly and peacefully. A judge in Barrie said recently, according to a report, that he had a prisoner before him who had spent more than half his years in prison. Because of the long years spent in prison, this man was unable to communicate with the court. He could not communicate, Mr. Speaker, as a result of the many years he had spent in prison. Do we want long prison terms to do this to people? If there is to be hope for us, society must have a better understanding of how to prevent crime. Second, we must provide an effective deterrent by imposing the shortest possible sentence in the circumstances. Unfortunately, what the shortest possible sentence is has not been discovered. We do not know how to prevent crime.
I cannot support the idea of long prison sentences taking the place of capital punishment. The cruelty of the long sentence is not in keeping with my philosophy, nor that of my riding of Simcoe North.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will intervene briefly in this debate. It has been a long debate and I know hon. members are trying to keep their speeches short. I intervene to indicate that, as Minister of Justice, I support the statement made by my colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), in this House when he began the debate on May 3, as reported on page 13088 of Hansard. In introducing the bill, he gave a long and thorough exposition of the reasons why it is being introduced and why at this time we feel capital punishment should be eliminated from the law.
Capital punishment has been debated in this House four times in the last ten years. It seems to me, with all due respect to what many have said in the four debates, that the real issue facing parliament and the country is not the issue of capital punishment: the real issue is how best the criminal justice system can be made most effectively and adequately to protect society. The issue is not whether we shall execute one, two or three prisoners a year: the issue is how the whole criminal justice system, the Criminal Code,

the administration of that code in our courts, the legal system, police enforcement and prevention systems of the country can best be made to work and protect our society and its values.
Quite apart from my personal opposition to capital punishment, I am convinced, beyond any shadow of doubt, that even if all murderers convicted of capital offences in the past ten years had been hanged, this would have done nothing to prevent the increase in violent crime which we have experienced in this country in the last few years. During the past 14 years, Mr. Speaker, in 70 per cent of all murders the suspect and victim were related or had some kind of social relationship. In my view, the prospect of hanging in no way influenced whether or not a capital offence in those cases was to be committed. Another 10 per cent of murders were committed during the commission of some other crime such as robbery, arson or sexual assault.
The execution of a few murderers will not deter crimes of passion, murder by sexual perverts, or gangland killings involving hired "hit-men." It will not stop violence. In my view, the very fact that there is on the law books a provision calling for the hanging, every year, of one, two, three or more people for the offence of capital murder gives our society a false sense of security and diverts us from what ought to be the real issues concerning the criminal justice system. To support my view, I wish to quote briefly, as my colleague the Solicitor General did, the words of Sir Robert Mark, the 38-year veteran of police work in Britain and current commissioner of the London metropolitan police, better known as Scotland Yard. Addressing the Canadian association of chiefs of police in Canada last summer, he said:
I am therefore opposed to the death penalty and so are most of my senior and most experienced colleagues, simply because its continuance prevents the reforms necessary to increase the effectiveness of criminal justice.
That is my position. It seems to me that the best and most effective deterrent to any crime, murder included, is the certainty of apprehension and the certainty of conviction. To bring about that certainty requires, under our system, better methods of crime prevention, crime detection, apprehension of criminals, and reforms of procedures in our criminal courts so that the determination of guilt and innocence is carried out more effectively and without the prolonged delays which so often are the case now. It seems to me that significant improvements must be made to our criminal justice system if that system is to serve its central purpose, the protection of society. That is why the government last July introduced the bail reform bill to which I introduced further amendments in October which became effective on April 26.
We introduced amendments specifically designed to make the bail laws of this country more effective, to protect society against those charged with murder, to protect society against repeaters within the criminal system, and against those who traffick or conspire to traffic in narcotics and who are responsible for up to 70 per cent of all crimes in our centres of population, including the crime of murder. And that is why the government introduced Bill C-83 which is now before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
June 14, 1976

That bill contains measures concerning gun control. There are to be greater penalties for the misuse of firearms, greater abilities for the police to deal with criminal elements using or possessing firearms, improved measures to keep firearms out of the hands of those who should not have them. Also, we included in that legislation-which I hope will be reported back from the committee shortly- measures to allow for the isolation from society of those deemed, by the legal process, to be dangerous offenders. They are to be separated from society for long periods. Bill C-83 also provides for the tightening of rules relating to the temporary release of criminals from prison. It provides for a more effective parole system, by which I mean that there is to be a more effective way of keeping within our penitentiaries those whom it is considered unsafe to release.
There is to be more effective examination of prisoners seeking release in order that we may release those who may safely be let out and participate in society. Included in that measure are controversial proposed changes with regard to electronic surveillance, or wiretapping, by police authorities after appropriate judicial authorization has been obtained. They are designed to strengthen the ability of police forces in this country to wage a more effective offensive against the bosses of organized crime who hire others to kill and often are instrumental in bringing people into the criminal system.
Later this week, as I said in the question period, I shall discuss with the attorneys general of the provinces other measures which will further improve the administration of our criminal justice system. The changes in the penalties for murder contained in Bill C-84 are related to the earlier measures I mentioned. The very stiff, no-pardon provisions will protect society by ensuring the prolonged incarceration of the convicted murderer. As I have indicated, the central purpose of our criminal law and administration of justice is the protection of society. Society has a right to be protected. It has a right to perceive that the criminal justice system is protecting it. That is why the long prison term provisions are there. They are, in fact, to protect society, to give society what it must have out of the legal system-that is, a perception or feeling that the system is serving to protect them, their communities and their values.
That is why the central issue in this debate is not whether we in this country hang one or two criminals; the central issue is whether we can build a more effective criminal justice system which, without hanging, protects society. It is my view that we can. The fact that we have a law relating to capital punishment gives our society a false sense of security, a sense of security that is undeserved. We should be addressing ourselves instead to how we can improve our criminal justice.
During previous debates on the capital punishment question, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) has made very distinguished and important contributions. It disturbed me to read his speech of the other day in which he indicated that he is reversing his position in order to ensure that capital punishment remains for treason. The incidence of treason in this country is extremely
Capital Punishment
low. In fact, Louis Riel was the last person hanged for treason-and that was in 1885.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert has had a long and distinguished career as a lawyer, as a member of this House, as prime minister and as an avowed supporter of the abolition of capital punishment. I hate to think that on the current bill he will be voting against sending it to committee. If he feels so strongly on the particular point that he has raised, because of his long-standing support of the abolition of capital punishment and his long-standing belief against hanging-which I have always taken to be a sincere and deeply-held belief-his proper course of action, knowing his long work in this area, would be to ensure that this bill is referred to committee. If he then wanted to suggest in the committee that there be some change in the bill, that would be the proper parliamentary course of action for someone who feels so strongly about the question of abolition as the right hon. member for Prince Albert.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
There are others in this House who are thinking of making amendments, and some who still have some doubts on the issue. I hope they will see the logic of my persuasion and will vote for the bill on second reading in order to put it into committee where their amendments can be considered or their doubts resolved through debate. I suggest, with the greatest deference, that would be the proper parliamentary course.
As I mentioned earlier, as Minister of Justice my chief concern must be the protection of society. It should be the concern of all members when they consider the measures now before the House. I am satisfied that the sentencing provisions contained in Bill C-84, together with the other initiatives we have taken and are taking through the measures introduced by the Solicitor General and I in Bill C-83, changes in the Bail Act and discussions we are having with the attorneys general as to improvements in the criminal justice system, are an adequate response to the need to make the criminal justice system work better for us and for its central purpose, the protection of society. That is the central issue in this debate.
We are not going to protect society by giving it a false sense of security by hanging one, two or three people a year. We are not going to make our criminal justice system more effective by all the debate, energy and thought that for so many years have gone into the issue of hanging. We should devote that same time, energy and thought to reforming our criminal justice system, to providing better methods of crime prevention and detection. The only effective deterrent there is to crime is the certainty of apprehension and conviction. That is the central issue in this debate and the debate on Bill C-83. It is the job of myself, this parliament, the provincial attorneys general and those responsible for the administration of justice to address themselves to that issue, rather than the capital punishment issue. They should address themselves to how we can develop better methods of crime prevention, detection, certainty of apprehension, and conviction.

speechtext: As I understand the question, Mr. Speaker, 1 do not agree with it. Obviously, police officers get into situations where they have to act to protect their lives or the lives of others. The minister says Canadians feel a false sense of security when they talk about capital punishment. I do not think this is true at all. I think they believe that for too long the government has failed to recognize its responsibilities in this area. Canadians do not feel a false sense of security. When I think of that kind of response from a child, when I think of the brutalizing of children, and when I think about our concern for the victim-which so rarely seems to be expressed-I think it is time people of that ilk started to pay the supreme penalty. I have no hesitation whatever in saying that society simply does not need these mad dogs. Society knows full well that these people are beyond the pale, and 25 years in jail is not going to contribute anything to their recovery.
Today, in cities such as New York we see apartments and office buildings under security, with armed guards and wire fences. The same situation exists in Philadelphia and Chicago. How far are we away from this situation in Canada? How long will it be before we see this kind of security escalate in Vancouver and Montreal? How long will it be before we see security escalate in the House of Commons? In my view, we are progressively moving into jungle warfare, with criminals having declared an open season on innocent victims. The question is: Should we stand idly by, or should we begin to fight? Are we going to allow this guerrilla warfare to overwhelm us, and turn the other cheek?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in the House on such an important matter as Bill C-84 which among other things deals with the abolition of the death penalty in Canada.
In connection with the decision of any hon. member on this matter, it seems to me that in our system we are not delegates to Parliament but members elected to Parliament. If we want to establish a system aimed at sending delegates to Parliament, to a democratic assembly, then those individuals would have to vote, according to the specific mandate given to them, this is another thing. But under the present system, a member must obviously listen to his own electors, his fellow citizens, even try to find their position and understand them, but having done that he ought to take the decision.
If the issue involved changing the system, I would oppose it because, in my opinion, a member of Parliament must have a political conscience, a social conscience, and he must be concerned especially by those issues. Mr. Speaker, this leads me to a remark made by my predecessor while concluding his speech. He said, and I heard him clearly, that 90 per cent of his voters were in favour of the retention of capital punishment. I would ask him how can he come to such a conclusion. speechtext: I probably would have come to that point. I am happy that the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) is so interested in my speech that he anticipated what I was going to say. I think we live under a system in which issues like this one should not have to be decided by a referendum.

speechtext: A short while ago I was speaking about the social and political conscience of members of parliament in our system. In my view we are elected to consider these questions, to study them, to listen to the Canadian people-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
-and to search for their views, but once we know those views we should have the courage to decide what we think is right or wrong and we should have the courage to make up our own minds on this question.

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that under our system a member of Parliament is not a delegate to Parliament, but he is elected, and when the constituents in his riding elect him, they are sure he will listen to them, he will try to understand them and he will truly represent them in the House.
I have listened seriously and very attentively to all the arguments coming from my constituency. I have even tried to understand more fully the position opposed to mine, I mean the position advocated by those in favour of the retention of the death penalty since I support this bill and may be described as a total abolitionist. Yet I have tried to understand the position of those opposed to this legislation.
In my opinion, the views I have heard fall into three categories. First, there are those who, as a matter of conscience, are in favour of capital punishment, those for whom it is a matter of morality, of religion, a spiriual matter, a matter of conscience and who are proclaiming: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. I am referring to those who believe that society should, in revenge or otherwise, take the life of those convicted of having taken someone else's life, the circumstances being taken account of, and the circumstances in their position, of course, can vary depending on whether the murder is qualified or not. To that group I must say that I have the duty, not only as a member of this House but also as a citizen, to accept and respect their point of view, and I respect it. I never tried to convince someone who tells me that he believes in conscience that capital punishment is not only a solution, but is acceptable in Canada or elsewhere. I respect that point of view.
As for the second and third groups, however, after discussion I found that their position is less based on conviction than on their intepretation of the facts, the law or the penalties. The second group is composed of those who believe that capital punishment is an effective deterrent to murder or crime. It seems to me that these people ought to
Capital Punishment
prove their point clearly before deciding in favour of capital punishment, because when you decide that the state must remove somebody's life, you have to make sure beforehand that the decision is fair. Nowhere in all the studies I have seen-I probably did not see them all but I did look into several of them-nor in all the arguments I have heard have I found anything indicating clearly that the death penalty is an efficient deterrent. Nothing indicates that clearly. Some studies seem to indicate that it is not an efficient deterrent. Opinions vary in this regard.
To my mind, it behoves those who claim capital punishment is a deterrent to prove their point, more so than those who claim the contrary. Until such time as an international scientific study is made, since all men are very much alike, until such time as I have seen such a study indicating clearly that capital punishment can be a deterrent, I must tell those people that they may be wrong.
A while ago I said that three groups want to retain the death penalty. The third is made up of those who are concerned about crime in our modern society, who are concerned about the fact that society does not seem to be protected well enough. Those people favour capital punishment but, very often, what they really want, is better protection.
They are told that in many cases, these are administrative matters, these are judgments made by civil servants, law officers of other groups. They are told that it is possible to amend some laws and to modify administrative procedures to ensure that those who are guilty of murder, individuals who are really sick from the social and human viewpoint, who have no control over themselves, are kept away from society.
And it is important to remind the House, and those people from the third group, of the change brought in for example by clause 21 of the bill. Clause 21 redefines the process through which first degree and second degree murderers will be eligible for parole. And I do not want to take the time of the House to read clause 21 entirely but I think we can sum up by saying that there is a fundamental and important principle to be considered in redefining first degree and second degree murder. And one of the important elements is that life imprisonment represents 25 years, for first degree murder and up to 25 years as well for second degree murder, depending on the judge.
About first degree murder, which is the planned or contract murder, there is an important change in the process of parole: the National Parole Board itself will no longer be able to realease anybody convicted of first degree murder, planned or contract murder before 25 years. That person will be released only through a commission of judges of the same court where he or she was found guilty and the comission will review his or her case after 15 years. Then and only them, after 15 years, will the judges be allowed to consider the eligibility for parole of the prisoner or the convicted person.
It is a major change because right now releases on parole are determined by a simple body such as the Parole Board which is made up of civil servants and full time commissioners and it is possible that this board, at least many think so, may not be so sensitive to the situation as are those whose responsibility it is to consider the eligibility of prisoners. If society undergoes a change, those persons
95 S70-15*72

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
may be isolated and as a result their judgment would not be reliable for other members of society.
The fact that judges are brought into the picture, that a panel of judges will decide on the eligibility of a prisoner beore the board considers his case is, I think, a fundamental change. Even if we did not have this 15 year minimum before judges may consider one's eligibility for parole, the judgment will remain very important.
Therefore I tell them that there are ways to protect society against dangerous criminals which might be released without being completely rehabilitated. Of course, there are other changes such as those in Bill C-83. Although we cannot hope to cover all cases, we are trying through firearms control to reduce at least the accessibility of dangerous persons to firearms and ammunitions.
I would like to point out another matter in this debate, which has often been discussed by jurists or legal experts because it is normal that the public, facing such a question, turn towards the legislators and ask them to find a solution. It is normal that the public exert pressures on politicians and say: We want you to solve this problem, we want you to try to fight crime in Canada and perhaps you may do so by reinstating capital punishment and particularly maintaining it.
It is normal because we have to be elected, we are known to people, they know that we sit in the House and it is thus normal that pressures be exerted on us. Consequently, it is normal that people require this from us. But one must not believe that all decisions concerning murders or any crime in any circumstances, in any region of the country, in any of the various sub-societies of all countries or in any of the various sub-cultures of our country, one must not believe that the House can pass whatever legislation which could, once and for all, ensure a balanced justice and fight crime or murder or make sure that murderers will never live out in society.
That is impossible to do. Why? Because by its very nature the system is in a way fragile, flexible, sensitive. For instance, the guilt of a person accused of murder is not determined by the law-makers, nor even by a judge. There is the question of the Crown attorney. How competent can he be? What kind of morality does he want to follow? What is his background and what kind of culture does he have? What are the views of the Crown attorney and of the defence attorney?
Many people know that the jury system can be influenced by the level of qualification or competence of the defence attorney. An emotional plea, for instance, by a defence attorney who is a better orator than an another attorney. It has often been heard that a poor person had been found guilty because he or she did not have the best lawyer. Some will say that we now have a judicial aid system and that no one will appear before a Canadian court without judicial help. That is true. However with the kind of society we are living in we will never be able to provide individuals without the necessary financial means with the best legal defence possible, we will never be sure that a judicial assistance system could assure them the best lawyer or the best legal defence possible.
There is, of course, the jury. It is an essential factor, sometime more important than any others. We want to 
have a supposedly sociological, political and social representation of the community to assume the judgement. Consequently, we are not the ones, as legislators, who have something to say but we bear however, the public pressures. We are not the ones who decide those issues. It will be the jury and the judge and it is, to a large extent, what gives its strength to our society, its flexibility but in some cases it can bring about a lack of unformity in sentences. The competence of the Crown or the defence attorney can decide the issue of a trial. Consequently, those factors will decide whether or not a person charged with murder or any other crime is guilty or not.
Mr. Speaker, I only want to answer those who stress before us the illness of our modern society, its weaknesses which make some individuals choose to commit criminal acts, to harm others, to attack them and even take their life. Faced with that problem, although we, as members of Parliament, are subject to public pressure because we are in the public eye, having been elected, society must not, nor must we believe that that problem can be solved, because even if Bill C-84 is defeated, even if all those people convicted of crimes, whether it be love tragedies, deliberate crimes or contract crimes, there is nothing that says that those who are charged with murder will actually be convicted of murder, precisely because of the jury system, because of the system of legal defence. I said earlier that nothing really proved that by applying the death penalty, even if it were applied to all people convicted of murder, first or second degree, or only even first degree, we can actually make sure that all people guilty of murder would be brought before the courts and convicted.
So I think, Mr. Speaker, that a factor in my decision is the fact that a mistake is always possible when it comes to judgments. I said earlier that there could be degrees of competence, that there can be an influence due to the environment, culture or history which may be quite different in Newfoundland and British Columbia because this is a diverse country. We live in a pluralistic society, so it is quite normal to have different points of view in different areas of this country. One must also take into account the degree of competence, the quality of the defence, the quality of the prosecution and the element of error. It is possible to have a better police force in one area of this country than elsewhere. It is possible for certain police elements to be more aggressive in one area of this country at a certain time in certain circumstances than elsewhere. The police in certain areas could be prejudiced against certain groups in society, and I think, Mr. Speaker, that is one of the major reasons why I cannot accept that capital punishment be acceptable to our society.
I do not see much difference between murder and capital punishment. I think the individual who takes away someone's life is a sick person, a person with something wrong. But I cannot accept that the state cold-bloodedly, after consideration, after legal defence procedure, after action by the police, action by the experts, the Crown attorneys, after all that, probably six months, one year and maybe two or three after the crime, society, the state can coolly decide to take someone's life. Mr. Speaker, I believe that this penalty is not useful, that it will not necessarily protect society, because the number of murders in Canada
June 14, 1976

is perhaps 10 or 20 times higher than the number of people who are found guilty by the courts. How can we say that the death penalty can really protect society efficiently?
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would like to say I am sorry that in this whole matter, in the House and elsewhere, we forget an important factor of criminality, we forget that there still are human, social and community conditions which result from human, cultural and often deep problems which contribute to violence. In poor urban or rural environments, young people of 14, 15 or 16 have known only bootlegging, drug trafficking, broken families, crime or other unpleasant things. If someone starts on the road to crime at 14, 15 or 16, I wonder if he should be the one to be punished.
I would hope that society, instead of emphasizing punishment, would try to show him that there may be some people who love him, that society is not limited to the environment he has lived in. I find there is within society as a whole a lack of understanding, delicacy, common sense, kindness and love for teenagers who are living in some environments. If we had not known something else, we would most probably do the same.
Mr. Speaker, to conclude, I urge the House to pass this bill because it is in my view a humane measure, one which says that the state cannot coldly take someone's life, and which, when considered against other government administrative measures or legislation, says that whenever there are sick elements within our society, it should do everything in its power to find a humane, non-violent solution, designed to rehabilitate these people or at least their environment when their own rehabilitation is impossible.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have lost count of the number of times I have taken part, since 1957, in debates on this important subject. I can honestly say that this is not the most inspiring, nor the greatest of debates in which I have participated. I thought the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford)-because I am his friend, I think he will not mind my saying this-was less than inspired and less than inspiring when he attempted today to defend the bill. It is not for me to read another man's mind; but, I wonder if he has lost the confidence in this measure which some of his predecessors in earlier days displayed. I remember well, when we discussed amending the Criminal Code to provide for a five-year partial ban, thinking I would not be so narrow-minded as not to give the five-year conditional ban a chance. But we have not been given that five years and in that regard the government has made an egregious error.
I think, too, that many members of this House and many citizens of this country are troubled by the way this matter has been orchestrated, are troubled by the coupling of Bill C-84 to C-83 and the confession of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) that, in order to get as much as he could under the one bill, he had to include as much as he could in the other. This kind of calculated quid pro quo is hardly conducive to a high-level, inspirational debate on a matter of conscience. The fact that the minister found it necessary to make the confession is not helpful. I am convinced that
Capital Punishment
no matter how I decide to vote on this bill-and I have not yet decided-my vote will bring me no great feeling of pride or satisfaction, because the bill contains many things which it ought not to contain and the existing legislation contains many provisions which in my judgment are reprehensible.
I have always opposed the sort of idea central to legislation we passed last time. In most sections thereof we subscribe to the idea that capital punishment is not a deterrent, yet when it comes to dealing with murderers of policemen and prison wardens we say that it is a deterrent. In all logic, if the imposition of capital punishment is a deterrent, let it be applied. But let it be applied in the case of the little girl who was raped and murdered, of the old gentleman in the corner store who was robbed and killed, and in the case of the Canadian citizen who was the victim of violent assault leading to death. Logically, capital punishment is either a deterrent or it is not.
Clause 5 of the present bill disturbs me. It provides:
Every one who commits first degree murder or second degree murder is guilty of an indictable offence and shall be sentenced to imprisonment for life.
I am neither jurist nor lawyer; yet, surely, if we have learned anything from the advance of criminology, it is this: there is a vast difference between first and second-degree murder. I do not like this little extra provision thrown in for the so-called hardshells in order to make the bill more palatable for them. I wish, sir, I could be in that easy position of some of my colleagues and stand up and say, "I am against the taking of life on moral grounds and for moral reasons, and the taking of life by the state is a sin." I do not believe that. If I were convinced that the taking of life by the state would make society safer and the lives of citizens more sacred, I would subscribe to no moral code which would prohibit my allowing that to take place.
Nor am I in that other happy category of those who say, "Hang them all, the short and the tall; that is the way to make society better." It would be easy to say it, but I don't believe it. Nor am I in that other category of those who say, "My constituents say, do thus and so; therefore I must do thus and so." I agree with the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) that in the final analysis we have to make our own judgment and we have to live or die politically by the exercise of that judgment.
I want to say how very much I was moved by the speech of my seatmate, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Kynard), one of the great medical practitioners of this country. I was much moved by his thoughful considerations respecting the whole matter of life expectancy of those who are under duress of state action. I was much moved by the eloquent address of my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), one of the articulate and sincere members of the party who in my judgment has a great contribution to make to Canadian public life. However, as is well known, we in this party enhance our reputation one with the other and our regard one for the other by the candour of our remarks, and I would disagree with him on one matter. I refer to the suggestion that the Palestinians, or PLO, are terrorists or that the PLO is

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
responsible for the dreadful and heinous activities at Munich.
While I could be critical of the Solicitor General, I will not suggest that anything he is doing in his advancement and manoeuvrings in respect of this measure is in any way connected with making it easier for terrorists. In fact, I sometimes criticize him, through his department, for making life a little too difficult for a lot of innocent Arab people who, with good intent in mind, want to come to this country.
We have to try, with this measure, to make a clear, conscience-based judgment. I regret the bill makes that difficult. I would be happier-and I have never been a starry-eyed abolitionist-had the government come forward without coupling gun control, without throwing in the tough penalty for second-degree murder and all these extraneous things and asked us to make a judgment. I think it would have been a more meaningful and a more intellectual exercise.
Underlying the whole aspect is that no matter how we talked in the last decade and a half, it really did not matter. The government, through its executive clemency, made this a de facto abolitionist country no matter what hon. members said or thought. This has entered into the whole discussion an object of resentful unreality, if I may call it that.
The Solicitor General this afternoon indicated what I have said for a long time. While technically we are engaged upon a free vote, it is in fact something less than a free vote. He suggested that, naturally, he could not produce argumentation on the other side of the question. If this were a free vote, a mere testing of parliament, why would he not? I sat in this House when we discussed this measure when it was a private member's bill. That is the way it should be today if it is truly to be a free vote.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I have said many times, and I say it with endearment to my beloved whip, there are too many votes on which the whip is on. This parliament should express itself on many, many issues without the whip being put on. Naturally, I exclude the budget speech and the Speech from the Throne. However, when you have a measure brought in by an individual minister, knowing full well the whole cabinet is going to abide by the law of cabinet solidarity, which the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) may forget occasionally, but not for long, you do not have a 100 per cent free vote. It is not right to suggest to the Canadian people that that is what is taking place.
Generally, this debate has been on a high level. However, I do not think this issue has been helped much by rumours that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Solicitor General would resign if it did not go through. That makes it too close, not only to being a government measure but a political measure. If I were not holding my conscience in very close check, I would be tempted to vote against the measure for these reasons. However, I think that would be wrong. They have no right to say on the left hand, the weaker hand, that it is a free vote, and on the right hand that they will resign if it does not go through and have cabinet solidarity laid down.

The debate generally has been on a high level but there are two aspects which I have resented all the way through. I do not appreciate retentionists telling me that because I do not support the return of the noose 100 per cent, in some way I am supposedly helping the criminals, that I do not believe in law and order and that I like all these rotten stinkers who make society a hell for decent people. On the other hand, I do not like to have it suggested to me that all civilized, sophisticated people are abolitionists. I do not think that is the case. This is an exercise through which we must move our way carefully and intellectually, guided by the fullest possible information available and by our own feelings as citizens who want the safest, freest society for our people.
I would be quite prepared to stand up and call for the reinvocation of the death penalty if I could be convinced that by that means society would be safeguarded and the rights of the individual would be more secure. I have been looking for many years for that evidence. It is that evidence that I find great difficulty in obtaining. I do not know whether the findings of Mr. Justice Branca have been put on the record. If they have, I will say that I agree with them and support the hon. member who put them down before. In a very brilliant speech to the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews, in British Columbia not long ago, he gave a little catalogue of countries which were abolitionist and countries which were retentionist. He gaVe the murder rate as follows. In 1965 it was 2.8 in abolitionist countries and 4.95 in retentionist countries; in 1966, 3.45 in abolitionist countries and 5.9 in retentionist countries; in 1969, 4.0 in abolitionist countries and 7.0 in retentionist countries; in 1970, the latest figures available, 4.65 in abolitionist countries and 7.65 in retentionist countries.
Noting the dreary and dreadful indication that it is increasing terribly in most countries, I cannot draw the conclusion that the retention of the final penalty has in fact curtailed, limited or diminished the murder rate. This is a significant, stirring and saddening statistic. When I relate that as best I can with the anomalies and contradictions in the bill, I will try to make up my mind fully how I shall cast my vote on this very important subject.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of Bill C-84, the legislation currently before this House which, if passed by parliament, will introduce a new and significant phase into the criminal justice system of this country. This has been an extremely difficult decision for me to make, and I want to assure the constituents of my riding that I have reached it only pursuant to a great deal of discussion, research and careful thought.
There is no question that the preponderance of the voters of Scarborough West will disagree with the position I am taking in connection with this controversial aspect of social legislation. As a parliamentarian, I have no choice but to live with the knowledge that, having in the final analysis made up my mind against the justification of continuing with capital punishment legislation as a legitimate form of penalty, I am casting my ballot on this issue in a direction which flies in the face of the current trend of thinking, not only in the riding of Scarborough West but, quite clearly, across this great nation that we are all so proud to call our homes and native land.
All I can say to those I represent during this thirtieth parliament is that I have indeed considered very carefully each and every representation which has been made to me, whether in writing, in the course of the six public meetings held in Scarborough West in recent months on peace and security issues, or in numerous and often heated private discussions.
The problem, Mr. Speaker, is that I have also considered it part of my mandate and my specific responsibility, as an elected member of our nation's parliament, to conduct private research on the issue through those many facilities available to me and, as well, to listen carefully to those Canadians, including members of parliament, who have definite and well developed views on the opposite side of the issue. This research and these latter discussions, based as they were on circumstances in some ways uniquely available to me as a member of parliament, have led me through an agonizing period of indecision to one clear conclusion.
The conclusion I have reached is that the onus must fall on the supporters of capital punishment as a legitimate form of penalty in today's society to prove their point that the advantages to Canadian society to be gained from this brutal and violent form of punishment, one which is really nothing more nor less than a legalized form of state murder, be it by way of hanging or whatever other method might be evolved, outweigh the disadvantages that become
Capital Punishment
so obvious when the state is empowered through legislation to execute some of its members. Thus, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me, in spite of the feelings of my constituents on the question, that logic dictates I really have no alternative other than to support a Criminal Code in Canada which, in attempting to both make the punishment fit the crime and at the same time ensuring adequate protection to Canadian society from those who would do its members harm, moves away from the last vestige of state-sanctioned physical violence that still includes murder, killing, hanging, or call it what you will, as a desirable method of handling some of the more heinous crimes which may be committed from time to time. Surely we must not permit our governing authorities in this day and age to engage in this form of legal violence unless the benefits outstrip the detriments accompanying such action.
Let us examine what is really being proposed in the legislation. Whether we like it or not, there has been a de facto absence of capital punishment as a form of penalty in Canada since 1962. A similar situation has existed in Belgium since 1863, and in such countries as Germany, Finland, Italy, Mexico, New Zealand, Portugal, Sweden and Great Britain of more recent date. None of these countries has completely legislated the death penalty off their books; they simply refuse to implement it through various legal means available to them under their respective laws. That has been the situation in Canada. Our criminal Code provides that the Governor General has the authority to commute death sentences. The fact of the matter is that the cabinet must review the record of evidence and recommendations from a judge who orders the sentence of death.
On the basis of this review it becomes a responsibility of the cabinet to recommend to the Governor General whether or not the death sentence should be carried out. What has been of some concern is that all such reviews have resulted in deferral of dates of execution or outright commutation of the death sentence. What I believe is less understood and less appreciated is that there have been only six commutations since 1967, half of which concerns cases which came to cabinet with the jury's recommendation for mercy.
Mr. Speaker, one must ask why all these automatic checkpoints are built into the legal system. They are not there in the case of any other sentences. Are we afraid, as a society, to make an error? If so, why are we less afraid in the case of other penalties? Why have we in years past carried out the death sentence in such secrecy, with as few witnesses present as possible? Have we been ashamed of our actions? Why have the cabinet and governors general of this country not authorized any executions since 1962? Surely the answer is obvious. Those in positions of authority and responsibility in Canada-and, I might add, in most other western countries-have had a nagging and horrendous feeling that the process was brutally wrong. Therefore, they have simply avoided the responsibility by exercising those safeguards provided in the law to the fullest extent possible.
I have no particular sympathy for the man or woman who takes the life of a fellow citizen in cold blood, regardless of the degree of provocation save complete selfdefence. I really have no idea whether such persons can ever be completely rehabilitated or restored to society as

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
normal human beings. There may be some who will respond to treatment, but I fear a large number will not. On the other hand, I am concerned about the families of the victims and earnestly believe that our criminal justice system should direct far more attention to their needs. I intend personally to work toward seeking improvements in this area in the name of a just and honourable society. The point remains, however, that my concerns for the victim and his or her near and dear ones, plus my lack of any particular sympathy for the guilty man or woman, do not in themselves lead me to accept that, even if such persons may have lost their right to live in society in the normal way, the state somehow inherits the right to take away all possible vestige of life itself through the brutal and final act of hanging them until they are dead.
Mr. Speaker, the state can be empowered by its citizens to be the weapon or the instrument-depending on how you look at it-for any deed we may consider to be desirable and within the means of the state to perform. On this basis, the reinstatement of capital punishment could be argued to be acceptable even if it meant restoring physical structures for that purpose in some provinces where they have long since been destroyed, for the provinces are called upon to administer the hanging procedure; even if it meant reverting to condoning a violent form of punishment by the state at a time when society is supposedly searching for every available means to reduce the amount of violence in society; even if it meant going it alone, as it were, as a nation when most countries of the industrialized west have long since abandoned this form of punishment.
Yes, the state can be given this power and this authority, but the question before us today is whether or not it should be given such power when for nearly 15 years we have indeed limited the authority to such an extent as to almost encourage the governing bodies of the state to choose not to exercise the brutal legislation at all. We seem to have done everything we can over the years to support what might be referred to as almost a weasling-out attitude on the part of authorities so that they might virtually ensure a discontinuance of this act of execution. We have done everything, that is, with the exception of removing the penalty itself from the statute books.
I have stated my position on the issue and have indicated some of the rationale leading me to the conclusion that, in the context of Canadian society in the latter half of the 1970s, it is my view that the proponents of the death penalty must be prepared to support their case against the increasingly forceful arguments that prevail on the other side. I have mentioned, among the latter, the situation prevailing in other western nations, the de facto experience, as it were, in our own country over the past 15 years and the obvious reluctance of governing authorities actually to implement the death sentence for whatever purpose or reason.
I would like to move, now, to the argument as to why the death penalty is inappropriate. If we are to give the state the power to take the life of a citizen by legal means- whether or not they implement it is almost beside the point-then this authority must, as mentioned earlier, be based on the argument that the existence of such power will surely act as a deterrent against future crimes of a like

nature and/or that the carrying out of such a sentence is a suitable and appropriate form of retribution-that is "the punishment fits the crime" philosophy.
Let us look, first, at the deterrence aspect. A careful review of all available statistics reveals that at best there is an extremely marginal case to be made for the death penalty as a deterrent; and on the other side of the coin there is indication of a reducing rate of first-degree murders where capital punishment has long since been abandoned as a legitimate punitive measure. Looking back a few centuries, we see that during the 38-year period of the reign of Henry VIII in England, from 1509 to 1547, there were 72,000 executions in that country, or an average of about five every two days. Bear in mind the relatively small population of the country at that time. Obviously, these executions were having little or no effect on the number of crimes committed for which the death penalty was considered an appropriate punishment to fit the crimes of the day.
By the year 1810, some 300 years later, England had moved to the position where some 300 different offences were punishable by capital punishment. Forty of these offences related to the area of forgery alone. It was only through the intervention of the banking fraternity itself- with some 1,000 bankers presenting a petition to the House of Commons at the time of Sir Robert Peel-that most of the forgery offences were deleted from the list of offences punishable by execution.
The simple reason for the reluctance to move was the concern that the absence of the authority of the state to take the life of the offender would indeed lead to an increase in the number of crimes relating to forgery. It never happened, Mr. Speaker. After 150 years of debate, England ultimately passed an act of abolition in 1965. This was followed by a continuing decrease in the number of murders per 100,000 of population in each of the next six years, with the exception of one. A recent move to reinstate the death penalty, owing largely to the terrorism rampant in some parts of the country, was turned aside by the British House of Commons. At the time the Home Secretary argued simply that to bring back the death penalty would be wrong and counterproductive in the fight against violent crime and terrorist murders. So much for the deterrence argument. In my view it contains little or no substance.
I want to move now to the argument whether the reinstatement of the death penalty in Canada, bearing in mind its de facto absence over a 15-year period, would be just and appropriate as a form of penalty best designed to fit the crime of first-degree murder. Here we are referring to the retribution argument. In speaking to this aspect, Mr. Speaker, let me make one viewpoint quite clear-one that my six public meetings in the riding confirmed as being largely in tune with the thinking of the electorate-and that is the clear intent that capital punishment, if continued as a legitimate form of penalty in Canada, should be made applicable to all those convicted of first-degree murder and not simply restricted to the murder of prison guards and police officers. It is my understanding that the police officers themselves would share this viewpoint, and so would many constituents who were abhorred over the cold-blooded murder of a Scarborough taxi driver a year or
June 14, 1976

so ago. Thus, we are talking about the legitimacy of the death penalty for first-degree murders, period, with no restriction as to its limited application over a designated sector society.
It seems to me that the retribution argument must in itself be viewed from at least three aspects, Mr. Speaker. First, there is the age-old argument of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Surely this went out long ago. Philosophically, we might compare the teachings of the New Testament to this Old Testament concept. That, alone, is some 2,000 years ago. In the intervening period we have seen the disappearance of most sadistic and torturous forms of punishment imposed by various states in their endeavour, presumably, to relate the punishment more closely to the nature of the crime. Some people argued, at my public meetings, for a return of some of these crime-related punishments. However, by and large the most convinced retentionist does not argue in this vein.
Accepting this, why should we accept capital punishment as an appropriate form of penalty for the crime of murder? If we refuse to accept a violent form of state-instituted bodily harm, such as stretching, dismemberment, or, indeed, the cat-o'-nine tails in today's society as a fitting retribution for heinous crimes by the guilty person on the body of the victim, why continue to accept the violence of breaking a person's neck in two for a crime of murder? I have received no satisfactory answer to that question.
The second aspect of the retribution issue is the expressed desire to ensure an adequately severe form of punishment for what is undoubtedly the most brutal of all forms of crime-taking the life of another person. In my view, imprisonment for life may result in an even more severe form of punishment in many aspects than the relatively simple and "once and for all" aspect of hanging. There has been one recent and well publicized example of this, where a lifer being interviewed on television stated unequivocally that he would rather hang than linger on indefinitely behind bars with little hope of any form of normal life in the distant future. It seems to me that is a most forceful argument in favour of life imprisonment in that the guilty person himself looks upon it as a more severe penalty than the single and yet final act of execution.
The third aspect of the retribution argument relates to life itself and who should have the power or authority to take it away. The state grants each one of us the freedom under which we live, but it by no means is the instrument through which we were granted life. I would thus argue that the state is quite entitled to remove our individual freedom at any time we indicate an inability to use this freedom in a responsible manner, as in the case of the commission of a crime against another member of society.
However, this entitlement does not extend, in my view, to the taking away of life. That is a matter that should be more appropriately left in the hands of those responsible for giving it in the first place. Thus, I can readily accept the argument of a murderer having lost his right to freedom and a normal life in society. What I cannot accept is this argument being extended to the point where society
Capital Punishment
commissions the state as the appropriate authority, not only to ensure that the loss of freedom aspect is respected through the means of imprisonment but, further, that the state be empowered to take the violent step of dispossessing the guilty individual of life itself.
I have attempted to present my argument in a rational and logical manner, eliminating as much as possible the emotional aspect. Yet I know and respect the emotions that are generated among Canadians today, both in Scarborough West and elsewhere in the country, when they witness an increase in the area of violent crime in general and a seeming disinclination on the part of the courts and the justice system to act in a speedy and definite manner to apprehend and punish the offender in a suitable way. I share this concern and, in addition to prodding the government to give more careful consideration to the needs of the victim and his or her close family, I also intend to press for more concerned action in the area of speedy apprehension and trial of persons charged with crimes against other members of our society.
I also intend to watch carefully over provisions relating to the early release of those charged with more serious offences. Many of these aspects are covered in the legislation accompanying this bill, and I believe it is essential that both Bills C-83 and C-84 receive the approval of this thirtieth parliament as quickly as possible. This will enable Canadian society to take a major step toward securing a reduction in the extent of violent crime in our country.
While my stance today indicates my objections to capital punishment both as a deterrent and as an appropriate form of retribution in the context of today's society, I do not condone an overly lax or inattentive attitude to the frustrations of society and its law officers to the problems relating to inadequacies in the administration of our justice system.

We can debate that point, and there will be other speakers follow me who will refer to it. This is a government bill in so far as the cabinet is concerned. I am very much concerned about this matter in terms of the freedom of the vote.
The other thing which worries me is the attempt by the government and those who would ask us to support the bill to suggest there is some form of onus on those who would oppose the bill to justify the position they have taken or will take when they vote. We heard that this afternoon, and we heard it pretty well every day during the course of the debate. I am not questioning the good faith of those who argue for this bill but, quite frankly, I think that aspect of our affairs is completely reversed.
I recall in 1973, when we last dealt with this bill and when I came into the House for the first time, listening carefully to the speeches made at the time, listening carefully to the solicitor general of the day put forward the bill, and listening to those who supported him by indicating it was a reasonable and proper proposition at the time to ask this House to support a bill which continued the experiment of abolition of the death penalty which had gone on five years before. Those who supported the measure at that time also said there was a good case for continuing the retention of the death penalty for the murderers of policemen and prison guards who were murdered in the course of performing their duty.
That proposition was put to us on the basis of the evidence that existed at the time. I supported the bill at that time. But the question I must ask myself today, as a member of parliament considering this legislation and who must stand by himself to vote and decide, is whether the circumstances of our society to which this bill applies in terms of the death penalty are better or worse today, and whether in view of those circumstances I can in the exercising of my right to vote in this place change the position I took in 1973.
Quite frankly, I have thought and I have worried about it because I do not take any vote lightly. I have come to the conclusion that the circumstances are such that I cannot support the proposal by the government which would abolish the death penalty for the killers of policemen, prison 
guards and other people in authority acting in the course of their duty.
The interesting thing about this bill is that it does not make a different individual out of a policeman or prison guard as a person, but only relates to that person in the course of his duty. We ask something of prison guards, of policemen, of constables, of custodial officers, of wardens, of jailers, of keepers, of guards and of permanent employees of prisons, to use the words of the statute, that we do not ask of ourselves-that is, we ask them to enter into circumstances for our protection. If there is an argument to be advanced, or if there is a statistic to be advanced which would indicate that the position taken by the government in 1973 ought to be different in 1976, then I would like to hear it. Until I hear it, and until I can be satisfied that that position is changed for the better, then I think I am bound to be consistent with what I stood for in 1973.
Given the very limited circumstances in which we speak of retention as opposed to abolition, the other question that has arisen in the course of this debate is the whole matter of deterrence. What has happened in the course of this debate, and even this afternoon out of the mouth of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), is that we have heard arguments both for and against capital punishment as if we were talking today about a law which said that all murderers were to be hanged. But we have gone far beyond that. I say, with respect and with some deference, that it is coming quite close to intellectual dishonesty to use the arguments that would have applied in the day when we were discussing the first movement away from the death penalty, at a period of time when we are now discussing the death penalty as it applies to a very narrow class. That is the first point.
I have looked for, and I have not found, one statistic which advances or supports the limited position. We are asked to accept the argument that in no case is the death penalty a deterrent. I cannot believe that is so. I cannot bring myself to accept the position that in every case involving the death of persons in the cases I have described, which are set forth in section 214 of the Criminal Code, where there has been an opportunity, in a way perhaps of husband and wife, or businessmen dealing one with another, do not have the opportunity to premeditate and think in advance, the death penalty is not a deterrent.
It is my fate, I suppose, as best I can, with my training and background in the law as a defence counsel, and as a Crown attorney-and I am very proud to have served in both capacities-to have to put my feet in the shoes of the accused and ask myself, if this were me, would I be deterred by the knowledge of the penalty?

I stand corrected. If this were I, and I had a certain knowledge of the consequences, namely, the imposition of the death penalty, would I be deterred from committing a crime that would lead to that even? Looking at it personally, I have to say that I cannot conceive of a situation, given a level of understanding or given a level of sanity, in which I would not be so deterred and in which other people would not be deterred. So I believe it is a false argument to say that the
June 14, 1976

death penalty is not a deterrent, because I think there are cases where it is. If there are cases where it is, as I believe we can find, I think it is incumbent upon us to ask ourselves what we are asking of those who, as the Minister of Justice said, are acting in the protection of society. We should ask ourselves what they are undertaking, with the setting aside of the death penalty.
So far as the statistics are concerned, when we are dealing with a matter of this nature with respect to the number of murders that have taken place, it is my respectful submission that there is no statistic available anywhere to indicate the number of murders that have not taken place as a result of the consideration of the penalty. Surely, if lesser penalties are regarded as deterrents for lesser crimes, then the supreme penalty must be regarded as a deterrent for the supreme crime, the taking of human life. So, sir, I do not intend to support this bill.
Another matter which has come up in this House is the whole question of conscience. I refuse to accept that in one way or another votes taken by members of parliament on an issue of this nature are matters of conscience and that other votes are not matters of conscience. I think that in one way or another all votes taken by members of parliament are matters of conscience. While I would want to retain the independence of my own conscience, in terms of any vote I take, whether on capital punishment or otherwise, I cannot condemn, and I would not condemn, members of parliament who have decided that as a matter of conscience they wish to represent, in their vote, what they feel are the wishes of their constituents.
Surely, if a member wishes to represent the 100,000 or so people who sent him or her here, this is a matter for the conscience of that member of parliament. We are sent here to make judgments. We cannot confer on every issue with our constituents. We have to decide how we will vote, we have to decide on what basis we will vote, and we have to decide what will motivate us with respect to voting. I have not taken a poll in my constituency. I do not think I have to do that. I think I know my constituents well enough to know that in terms of their feelings about this piece of legislation and the issue of capital punishment they feel as strongly as any other group of Canadians.
However, with that feeling which I know exists, as a member of parliament I have to make a decision on the legislation which is put before me, on the debate I have heard and on the consequences, as I see them, if this bill passes in terms of the custodial people I have described. I believe we will be doing them and, indirectly, society a disservice if we do not make the proper decision. I do not accept the argument that the retention of the death penalty for the limited number of people it would affect in any way is exclusive to the whole issue of improving conditions in society. Nor do I accept that there is no place in our system of justice for the proper use of the royal prerogative of mercy. The emphasis has to be on the words "proper use".
I recognize too that there can be difficulties in terms of the trial of an accused. Mistakes can be made in the course of trials. Those mistakes can be made no matter what crime or accused is being tried. We might consider the
Capital Punishment
offence a lesser offence or a greater offence, but those are the vicissitudes which have to be faced in any human institution. The system of justice which we use in this country as it is incorporated in the Criminal Code in terms of criminal law and the appellate process is perhaps the best in the world, and if those aspects of the legal machinery should fail there is a place for the proper use of the royal prerogative of mercy. I think that if there is any doubt in terms of whether an accused was properly identified, whether evidence was admitted which ought not have been admitted, whether there was some question of the mental balance of the accused, or a host of other matters which might arise in a capital case, then no one who is reasonable in this country could condemn a cabinet for exercising that royal prerogative of mercy.
I know that generally cabinets in the past-and I assume cabinets of the future will do so-perhaps took more time with respect to commutation matters than other matters which might have come before them. The cabinet decision has a profound effect on the life of a human being, and that is as it should be. However, the responsibility to administer the law and to act in accordance with the law is an important one. What has happened, unfortunately, in the operation of our system is that there has been a suspicion abroad that government decisions have been based more on how ministers feel-although perhaps honestly and strongly-than on administering the law. I hope that that is not so because I do not believe we should be subject to the rule of man but rather we should be subject to the rule of law.
This is not a very easy speech for me to make, and it will not be an easy vote for me. I am not a violent person, but I believe that there is a case to be made for the retention now in the law on the basis of the deterrent effects the death penalty can have on those who have an opportunity to think about what they are doing, and having had that opportunity, go ahead and act anyway. It is because of that very important aspect of premeditation that the present law ought to stand and that this bill should be defeated.
I respect the opinions of those who differ with me. I am sure that those who differ with me feel as strongly as I do. I believe that this House should come to a decision fairly quickly with respect to this matter, subject to the right of each hon. member who wants to speak on the principle of the bill to do so.
I had not intended to speak at all in the course of this debate, but after I read and listened, I felt that I had to rise and put my position as honestly, fairly, succinctly and as briefly as I could, and I want to thank the House for its respectful attention to what I have had to say.
