The chief motivation I have for voting for the bill is my respect for human life. There is a lot of opinion on this side of the issue and I think some of it is best expounded by the various churches. I think the largest group of public opinion that makes the point on this side of the issue comes from the churches, and I should like to read some brief statements by the churches that back up my statement. Bishop G. Emmett Carter, President of the Canadian Catholic Conference, states:
Parliament should abolish the death penalty and "bring about the reforms which are necessary in our penitentiary system and in all areas of justice.
A society which really respects life cannot use the death penalty to protect itself and at the same time create an atmosphere wherein other human rights will be respected. Moreover, violence engenders violence and the death penalty is a violent act. The spirit of the gospel is one which leads us to favour mercy and clemency."
The seventeenth General Council of the United Church of Canada states:
We affirm our belief that capital punishment is contrary to the spirit and teaching of Christ.
The statement of the Anglican Church, written by Dr. Leonard Hatfield, is equally profound:
Surely the taking of life is not conducive to the recognition of the worth of the individual and the consequent protection of society.
There can be no question about the unfortunate influence of an execution upon many other persons. For instance, prisoners often identify themselves with the condemned person. They see in his death the

ultimate rejection of those who through life have been rejected by society, so they hate society the more.
There are just some of the statements. I could go on. There has been a lot of debate about whether capital punishment is a deterrent. I think if people read with an open mind and and open heart all the information that is available they should be convinced, as I am, that no case can be made for taking a man's or woman's life as a deterrent to murder. It just is not so. You can look at the statistics and consider the body of opinion and you will see fluctuations and changes from year to year all around the world.
Countries that have been abolitionist have shown fluctuations, and countries that still use the death penalty have shown wide fluctuations in their views. One year the statistics would be very high and another year they would be very low. If you look at the so-called murder graph, if you want to put it that way, in terms of countries that are retentionist versus countries that are abolitionist, it comes out very clearly on the side of those countries that are abolitionist.
In 1975 the murder rate in abolitionist countries was 2.8 per 100,000 population; in the retentionist countries it was 4.95 per 100,000 of population. In 1966 the figures were 3.45 abolitionist, 5.9 retentionist; in 1967, 3.25 abolitionist, 6.35 retentionist; 1968, 3.9 abolitionist, 6.7 retentionist; in 1969, 4.0 abolitionist, 7.0 retentionist, and in 1970 they were 4.65 abolitionist and 7.65 retentionist. I think these figures show very clearly that taking a human life is not a deterrent to murder.
One of the fears that many of my constituents have is that people get out on easy parole terms and I must say I have been somewhat concerned about that as well. I am glad to see that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has taken steps to change the law so that there is really no such thing as easy parole.
I am also pleased to see a clause in Bill C-83 that would deal with the habitual criminal. Criminologists and others who deal with the penal system know very well that there are some people who can be described as an accident looking for a place to happen. These people will no longer be turned out into society if it can be shown that they really are in the category of an accident looking for a place to happen. They just will not ever get out again. I think that is fine, because society must be protected. That is what Bill C-83 and Bill C-84 are all about-the protection of society. We must be concerned with it, and we must find the best way possible to protect society against violent crimes.
From 1920 to 1974 182 persons were granted parole often a death sentence. Only 14 had their parole revoked for misbehaviour, and only nine of these had again committed an indictable offence.
Between 1867 and 1975, in the entire history of our country, only one who had his death sentence commuted committed a second murder. These are pretty substantial bits of evidence that the death penalty is not a deterrent.
I said in the beginning that I was not going to speak very long, and I shall not, as I think there are other members who wish to speak. I just wish to reaffirm my position that I shall vote in favour of Bill C-84. I do not think there is
June 14, 1976

any place in a civilized society for the death penalty, and it should be abolished.

Mr. Speaker, I for one was not going to enter this debate until I saw some of the tactics being used by the government to manipulate the House into an early passage of Bill C-84. As a result I have reviewed the situation, and tonight I should like to say a few words touching first of all on the whole question of urgency. Why does the government seem to feel it is so urgent that this legislation be passed quickly without, I would suggest, due committee review, and before the House recesses?
I say that because the last time we dealt with this general question was in the last parliament. It was only in December, 1973, that we passed Bill C-2. It provided the limited continuation of the death penalty, until December 31, 1977. You will recall that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) almost pleaded for the bill to be accepted; he said he needed extra time in which to gather statistics in order to make a meaningful review. He was concerned about an 18-year review, and specifically about figures relating to the periods 1956-62, 1962-68, and 1968-74. He made a good argument at that time.
Having read the minister's most uninformative statement as reported in Hansard, and the 55-page statement which was not reported in Hansard but which was delivered outside the House on the same day, I conclude that the minister glossed over certain statistics; which were allegedly, the very reason for his wanting an extension of the provisions of Bill C-2 to which I have already referred.
The minister indicated that the murder rate per 100,000 of population rose from 1.2 in 1962 to 2.4 in 1974. He included these facts in the statement, made in this House and outside. But he did not point out that in the previous six years the murder rate had remained static at about 1 per 100,000 for the period ended 1962. In those previous six years it hovered at approximately one per year, and the significant increase in the murder rate occurred in the last 12 years.
I believe, as does my party's House leader, that if the government was serious about allowing a free vote on the bill the Solicitor General would have presented as ably as possible all statistics bearing on those three six-year review periods to which I previously referred. Therefore the first point with which I wished to deal this evening was the question of urgency. There is no urgency.
Second, I wish to touch briefly on the 55-page ministerial statement to which I alluded earlier. I shall quote certain parts of that statement to show that it contains conflicting positions. Before I do so, I wish to deal with this general proposition: is capital punishment a deterrent? I shall review the experience of other countries.
Contrary to what the Liberals and socialists like to think, there is no stampede on the part of the world's nations in the abolitionist direction. States are not stampeding to become abolitionist. Certainly United Nations records make that clear, records prepared by United Nations officials who themselves, obviously, are abolitionists, show capital punishment is increasing. They

state, in despair, that the nations of the world are increasingly imposing the death penalty, that such imposition is on the increase, not on the decrease. I point out that the Communist states of the world are uniform in retaining the death penalty. Not one has done away with the death penalty; yet those in this House who espouse the virtues of some of those states say we should be abolitionists.

I suggest it has everything to do with it. This is a government bill and the fact is that there will not be a free vote. The government does not have the courage to tell the Canadian people that it is trying to inflict abolition on the nation against its will.
Before the House rose for dinner I mentioned that in my view for democracy to flourish it should continually evolve. I believe it essential that public opinion should be allowed to express itself. I said our system had developed certain rigidities, a situation which is presently allowing a minority, in this case a minority of abolitionists, to assert its will over the majority of Canadians. The parliamentary system is allowing this because there has been so little change in that system over the past century.
Governments have learned that by catering to minorities they can secure re-election and deal harshly with certain sections of public opinion. They have learned that they can frustrate the will of the majority-it is just the question of choosing the right time. In the view of the administration, this is an opportune moment, about two years away from the next election, to inflict abolition on the state. That is one of the issues I intend to deal with tonight.
Few electors in this country can comprehend the degree of power held by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today, though many senior officials in the public service and his intimate advisers do. Oscar Wilde's quip, made some 80 years ago, that democracy meant simply the bludgeoning of the people by the people might well be an apt description of the government's approach to this legislation. It appears that between elections there is little need to court public opinion. After an election date is decided upon, the wooing process begins. New programs are offered with
June 14, 1976

particular appeal to vocal minorities. Regional interests are championed. Stress is laid on proposed new handouts with little mention of their eventual cost to the public at large.
Once re-elected the government is subjected to little restraint or discipline. With a majority in parliament, it is supreme. This situation has arisen here and elsewhere after 30 years of Liberal-socialistic rule in western democracies. Those who once were reformers, who indeed sought democracy, have become unresponsive to the wishes of today's majority and impatient with the democratic process itself. They now use our parliamentary institution as a device to impose their minority views on the majority. They are confident the next election will turn little on today's issues and more on personalities and the floss of the day. Examples of this attitude are numerous.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), leading spokesman on this bill for the NDP contingent in parliament, speaking in favour of the government's bill to abolish capital punishment, sums up his thinking when he says, as reported at page 13096 of Hansard for May 3, 1976:
I regret that so many people in our society misunderstand and think that they have the right, because they believe they have a majority, to decide how we should vote.
I hope all members noted the odd terminology used by the hon. member for Greenwood while, in effect, seconding the passage of this bill on behalf of the Solicitor General.

speechtext: You hate democracy.

That is right. The hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Abbott) said "They hate democracy." The hon. member put it very well. If he reads what the hon. member for Greenwood said a little later on he will find he elaborated on this question of how parliamentarians should relate their votes to the wishes of their constituents.
I would draw attention to the fact that the Solicitor General took the same tone with respect to this bill as did the hon. member for Greenwood, saying-as can be confirmed by reference to page 44 of the prepared text of his speech-that somehow or other members should sit in this House and vote according to their own consciences or according to their own convictions, in spite of evidence that the public will would have them do otherwise. Both those hon. members referred to Edmund Burke, a Conservative, to justify their stand on this issue. Mr. Speaker, Edmund Burke is a well-known authority, but surely for two members, the minister and the hon. member for Greenwood, to suggest we should be bound by the views of a Conservative politician 202 years ago is absolutely ridiculous. I question whether either of them troubled to check out the situation in England at the time the speech to which they were referring was made to the electors of Bristol in 1774.
At that time, when Burke spoke of his role as a member of parliament, the total number of people who were actually able to vote in England was less than 100,000. Members were in fact elected through "pocket boroughs" and other cozy arrangements; the age of widespread enfranchisement in England had not yet been reached. When Burke spoke, the population of England was some seven million. Means of communication were sketchy. There was, of course, no radio, no telephone network, no television. There was no
Capital Punishment
way in which the public at large could be rapidly informed concerning the issues of the day.
What I find interesting is that when members opposed to abolition quote from the Bible or from other religious sources concerning capital punishment, the response from the other side is always, "Do not take those statements out of context." Yet this is exactly what those very members have done with respect to Edmund Burke's comments. What he was saying was merely this: he was asking the voters of Bristol to realize that when he went to Westminster they should not expect him to vote only in the interests of the electors of Bristol but, rather, that they should expect him to vote in the interests of the nation as a whole.
Put in a different context, he was saying that when a member is elected from Toronto he should not be expected to go to parliament and become a protagonist for the interests of Toronto as against, for example, the interests of Montreal or some other city. Edmund Burke was suggesting that we should sit here to consider the interests of the nation, not local issues. If I may quote him directly, he said:
Parliament is not a congress of ambassadors from different and hostile interests; which interest each must maintain, as an agent and advocate, against other agents and advocates; but parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation, with one purpose, that of the whole;-
I hear the House leader applauding that.
-where, not local purposes, not local prejudices ought to guide, but the general good, resulting from the general reason of the whole. You choose a member indeed; but when you have chosen him, he is not member of Bristol, but he is a member of parliament.
I was hoping that the Solicitor General and the House leader as well as others on the government side would applaud that as they did, since they do not seem to know in subsequent years Edmund Burke said something entirely different. For example, in his speech in 1780 on the economical report Edmund Burke had this to say, and I would draw it to the attention of the Solicitor General he said that the people are the masters.

At page 9 of this updated report of the United Nations, Item No. 48 states:
June 14, 1976

It remains extremely doubtful whether there is any progression towards the restriction of the use of the death penalty. Periods of abolition or non-use may be succeeded by widespread executions in a highly unstable political situation or by a sudden return to the death penalty as a sanction where a State feels insecure. Moreover, in a few States where serious forms of terror and violence have been experienced, the death penalty has been used increasingly as counterterror, or deterrence.
That is an interesting new conclusion in that report, and I invite hon. members to read both reports because I believe, unlike the Solicitor General's presentation, this report is a fair presentation of the state of the death penalty at this time around the world, written incidentally by abolitionists, in the sense that the United Nations has hoped for more abolition than there is presently in the world.
I mentioned earlier that I would like to touch upon certain provisions in the legislation. I was rather surprised that the Solicitor General did not give some type of overview of the various provisions, but I realize he should not be referring to them clause by clause. I would point out to hon. members that general impression has been created, that somehow when we adopt abolition there will be tougher parole laws and tougher treatment of those people adjudged guilty, but that is not in accordance with the facts as you will see if you read this bill. There are provisions dealing, for example, with time spent in custody. Before I read the bill carefully I did not realize that the minister contemplated that when he had written in the reference to a firm 15 years or 25 years, he meant it to be clear that the time started running from the time an individual was charged and not from when he was convicted.
Let me point out that there are three individuals awaiting execution on July 15, 1976. One was first charged in October 1971, the second was first charged in February, 1973, and the third was charged in June, 1973. I would think it reasonable to anticipate that a person could spend five years, perhaps, and certainly three, going through the various judicial procedures prior to final conviction, and that that time apparently would be included as part of the time to be served in prison.
There are two provisions I find particularly interesting. The first is a provision which allows the parliament of Canada to enact, by express reference to the act we contemplate passing, a new act freeing a man who has been duly convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. This is something I do not think the public fully understands. This bill does not just contemplate doing away with the death penalty by requiring a person to be imprisoned for life. Nobody need be imprisoned for life under this bill if he can get this parliament or a subsequent parliament to take up his case and enact a special act to spring him. For those who say that somehow or other a life imprisonment is worse even than hanging, let me point out that no one, even if he is sentenced to life, need despair because he can take up his case with the government or any member of this House who can try to secure his freedom through the passage of another act, making reference to the part I referred to in Bill C-84.

I accept the keenness of your hearing, Mr. Speaker. I would not disagree with the Chair's right to hear, as that is one of the few benefits that accrue to distinguished people like yourself who occupy that office.
Before I begin some of my comments I want to touch for a minute on some of the things said by other hon. members, including the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the hon. member who has just taken his seat. Before doing that I want to say simply and categorically that I intend to vote for the bill. I say that immediately to make it easier for those who do not want to stay and listen to my reasons, but who may wish to depart.
Having regard to the very valid suggestion by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), I believe we should consider very seriously the necessity of assuring that this bill receives second reading. Apart from some of the major issues in respect of which we may differ, the

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
parliamentary practice at the present time leads us to the conclusion that third reading is the stage at which we can best deal with a bill of this kind, that is, when we see it in its finished form.
There are those who feel some improvements ought to be made, and there are those who feel, as did the Minister of Justice, that if the people come to the conclusion that capital punishment is a suitable penalty for certain types of offences, they should have the right to attempt to obtain the approval of their colleagues in this House during the free vote, and that hon. members should have the right to move the kind of amendments that are available under our rules in an attempt to reach a consensus.
I say it once that I will vote for the bill as it stands. I like the bill as it stands, and I have been a constant opponent of capital punishment for well over 40 years. I would prefer to see the bill passed in its present from. However, if it were the will of this House, expressed by a majority that there be some exclusions, and I were driven very hard to it, I would sorrowfully and regretfully vote for such an amended bill. I hope it will not come to that. I hope we will have the chance to hear all of the proposals which might lead to amendments, deal with them in this House and in the committee, as we should, with the net result that the bill will come back in its present form for third reading.
On the question of a referendum I would refer hon. members to a very considerable speech made in the 1973 debate by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who dealt very extensively with this issue. He made quite plain in his speech that members of this House had a duty which was not consistent with a system of referenda. I will come to this again.
If we are to abdicate our responsibility I can see a situation in which we would watch carefully the statistics which come out from Statistics Canada. Members of this House would set their sights at objectives which Statistics Canada, or the polls taken by an institute of polling, would suggest indicated the course of conduct which at that particular time the peoplei of Canada would prefer the government to adopt. What kind of consistency of approach in respect of government would we have under those circumstances? My experience, Sir, over a very long period of time as a practitioner of law, as a soldier, and as a member of this House is that people do change their approach to a number of the problems they face.
Twenty-five or 30 years ago, I think a majority of the people in this country were opposed to capital punishment, for reasons with which I will deal briefly. The pendulum has swung since then. Now I think the majority of people for certain reasons favour the return of capital punishment. But there is nothing to suggest that 25 or 30 years from now the pendulum will not swing the other way. From my experience and my knowledge I suspect very strongly that this will be the case. Therefore while it is essential that any member of parliament or any person elected to office should have a very serious responsibility to consult with his constituents, to make shift and to understand their thinking, and to speak to and to listen to them-any elected member who does not recognize that responsibility is a fool and does not deserve to hold elected

office-I do not think this should mean that such a man may not exercise his judgment and discretion or be free to yield readily from time to time to the changing ideas, trends, and whims of a number of people in his constituency, or in the country.
I think in our approach to this issue we should be very careful. I made a speech in favour of the abolition of capital punishment well over 40 years ago in a church basement in a small community, where there were members from many denominations. I spoke in favour of abolition in a speech which was accepted. I never wavered in my support for the abolition of capital punishment. I have spoken on numerous occasions both in this country and elsewhere. Although it has not been a major issue in elections, certainly during the course of the 1972 election and the 1974 election I was asked on a number of platforms what was my stand with regard to capital punishment. I was able to reply simply that I stand where I have stood before, that is, that I am opposed to capital punishment. I told them I believe in abolition and if they elected me they would be electing me with that point of view. I was elected with a substantial majority in 1972 and in 1974. I feel, as I think any other member sitting in this House will feel who was asked the question and took the stand I did, that I came into this House with this format and can vote as I indicated my position at the time of the election.
Like on the other occasions on which we have discussed this momentus issue, this has been a marathon debate. I do not say this disparagingly, although I had hoped we could take a quick decision as was the case in the United Kingdom during the course of the last two debates they had. However, this is a matter of great concern. While it affects only a comparatively few people it goes to the wellsprings of our civilization, our society, our culture, and our religious beliefs. It certainly is an issue on which no one should be denied the right to speak. I have listened to some of the speeches made during the debate. I have read others.
I take my mind back to some of the debates in this House in the last 18 or 19 years by some of the great members and leaders. I spoke of the right hon. member for Prince Albert and his speech. I have heard the present and former leaders of our party make very excellent contributions, great speeches, in which they expressed their views on the subject. I have heard the leader of the New Democratic Party and its two preceding leaders on the issue. I have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the previous Prime Minister, the late Lester Pearson, speak on this issue.
I think one of the greatest speeches was one made by Arthur Maloney, now the Ontario ombudsman, who sat at that time in what was the rump of our party when we overflowed in those glorious days on to both sides of the House, a position which we are again rapidly approaching at the present time. He rose to his feet on a private members' bill, I think one introduced by the Hon. Frank McGee, and made one of the greatest and most eloquent and articulate speeches on this particular issue. Paul Martin, who was sitting in the House, told me that his opinion it was one of the greatest speeches he had heard on this issue. It convinced people. It is interesting to note that just a few weeks ago right in this House Mr. Maloney, with Bishop Carter, chairman of the Catholic Congress of Bishops, and other eminent people in this country who had
June 14, 1976

come here for a seminar, showed that he had lost none of his eloquence or his conviction that capital punishment must be abolished, and abolished permanently.
I have noted with interest that members on both sides of this House and on both sides of this House and on both sides of this issue have quoted from Scripture. I think it comes out even. I do not think it is necessary for me to quote from the Bible. This has been done by members on both side of the issue.
As I suppose have other members, I have received a number of letters containing quotations from the Bible. I have also received submissions from members of the public which dealt with different methods of execution. Some have recommended easy and painless methods. This, I think, would be quite difficult. In any event if it should be the wish of this parliament to have state executions become part of our social system, then it would be inconsistent with this wish to attempt to soften the effect by searching diligently for nicer, neater or tidier ways of killing that would be more acceptable to the condemned person.
I have pointed out before that I, as well as other members of this House, have appeared on behalf of a number of people, well over a score, who have been charged with murder. At various times during the course of briefing myself I took it upon myself to talk to them, previous to preparation for trial, to know their motivation, to know their purpose, to know what happened and how it happened. I think it is very essential to anyone who accepts the responsibility of defending a man or a woman charged with an offence which is punishable by capital punishment to do that. To that extent I suppose I have had a little better opportunity than quite a few people to make some clinical examination of the question of motivation.
People who spoke to me under those conditions in prison cells had no motive to conceal from me the true facts, and no reason to try to exaggerate their feelings, their viewpoints, and their attitudes, and I say to hon. members in this House that in not one instance of all those more than a score of people I talked to did it develop that the question of what might happen if they were caught, if they were convicted and if they were executed, enter their minds at all. That does not mean that it might not with regard to some people, but my observation of the people I spoke to, the people I had to consult with professionally, and the people whom I was charged with defending in a court of law, led me to the irresistable conclusion that the question of deterrence was not an issue which was in their minds at or immediately prior to the time their offences were committed. That is the clinical study which persuades me that there has been an exaggerated attitude and an exaggerated importance given to the question of deterrence.
The question of deterrence has been raised in a number of ways. For example, I noticed in a news report some months ago that those who were in favour of retention were able to given some prominence to statements made by two convicted murderers who said that, in their opinion, 25 years was a much harsher sentence than death, and that they would prefer to be executed rather than to sit out 20 or 25 years in jail. If that is the case, surely that gives the
Capital Punishment
lie to those who suggest that the death penalty is an adequate deterrent, because if in the minds of those two people, who are intimately concerned about this issue, 25 years is a greater deterrent-and 25 years is the penalty suggested in this legislation-then it speaks to me quite plainly. It says to me quite plainly that, if there is a deterrent, the deterrent is in the harsh prison sentence and not in execution by hanging.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Now I will refer to some of the comments made in the very excellent paper-I do not agree with the paper, but it was well put together-which was the submission of the police chiefs. As I read these submissions I came to the opinion that buried, but still quite apparent, in these various submissions was the attitude that these police people and those who presented briefs for them did not really believe philosophically that, in a general way, capital punishment was a deterrent. What they said about deterrence was very simple. If a man commits murder and if he is captured, tried, and executed, that is a deterrent in the sense that that man cannot commit another offence. That is the point they made from their observations, and I think they veered well away from the issue of deterrence generally. They were submissions which were full of candour, they were brief-mercifully brief-and well put together. As I say, they represented a point of view with which I very heartily disagree, but they expressed honestly and candidly the other side of the argument. I think the only conclusion one can draw from examining what they said and wrote is that capital punishment is not a deterrent generally in a philosophical sense.
Finally, Mr. Woodburn Thompson, who was engaged by the police chiefs, and whose brief was the last one to appear in their submissions, said that in his opinion, as a result of his examination, to use capital punishment as a deterrent was barbaric. That was contained in the submissions put forward by the police associations of Canada.
Now we come to another group of people, those who are generally abolitionists by nature, thought, and attitude, but who feel that it might be better to keep the punishment of hanging with respect to one or two certain specified offences. Personally I find it very difficult to follow such logic. If the fear of death is not considered to be an adequate deterrent to prevent potential murderers from committing one kind of murder, how can it be said that it would constitute a deterrent in respect of another kind of murder?
Are we to assume that human nature can be so compartmentalized that a person planning a murder for revenge, or a cold blooded killing for some monetary consideration, would not be deterred by the fear that he might ultimately be placed on a scaffold and hanged, but that a person considering killing a policeman or a prison guard, or committing treason, will stop, reflect, and tell himself, "I had better not commit this crime because, if I do, I will face the ultimate penalty"?
I just fail to reconcile the kind of logic which suggests that while I like to feel I am an abolitionist, and while I am generally opposed to the state taking life, yet it may well be necessary to leave open the right for the state to hang people for one certain type of offence. How can that be

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
reconciled with the belief such a person must hold that capital punishment is not a deterrent? And that person generally takes the tolerant and proper attitude that it is no more right for the state to take life than it is the right of any person to take life. I fail to follow that kind of argument. For this reason I hope that this bill will receive at least second reading, so that if there is an argument to be made by such people it will be made and presented in the normal course of events in the committee, and come back into this House so we will have the opportunity of considering it sensibly and logically.
Therefore I think this brings us down to the real nature of the argument, that is, the true character of capital punishment. Once inflicted, it has the clear and simple effect of preventing the person who will have been executed from committing another crime. There is no doubt that many people who are in favour of capital punishment are in favour of it for that reason. In my opinion it is a simple form of institutionalized state vengeance.
Let us be honest and face the fact that this sort of thing has always represented a very strong element in our social structure. I do not agree with it, I do not like it, but we have to be realistic and remember that it was only several hundred years ago when inanimate objects which accidentally brought about injury and death to people were dealt with almost as if they were criminals themselves. Those inanimate objects might have been sticks, stones or weapons. If a person met his death or injury because of some accident involving inanimate objects, these objects were put on trial. Later we had trial by ordeal, and the fact that the crime of treason was punishable by the convicted person being hanged, drawn, and quartered.
Five hundred years ago is a long time to us, even to some hon. members who have been in this House for some time, but it is a heartbeat in the life of a society, in the history of mankind, and the characteristics of those earlier days are not easily eliminated. Particularly is this so at the present time when we live in a state of frustration felt in a society which is badly fractured, which is fearful and annoyed by the apparent toleration and encouragement of permissiveness, by government which moves against rather than with the grain of human nature.
I feel very strongly that it is this fear, this anxiety, this frustration, this anger which in many cases constitutes the compelling reason behind what appears to be the bloodthirsty mood of the normally mild, reasonable, and moderate Canadian people. Many of the views and much of the opinion of those who favour capital punishment seem to me to be part of this anger and this frustration, and the noose has become a symbol rather than a remedy.
I think people who stand up and talk about hanging do so not because many of them want to hang people or put their hand on the hand of the hangman as he springs the trap which sends condemned people down to choke to death, but because they feel this frustration. They want the right for their families to walk the streets, they want security and stability in society, and the noose has been picked as the symbol which suggests to them some way of restoring the things they seek.

I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot do anything but vote for this bill on the basis of such arguments as this. There has been a sort of mythology grow up that those who are in favour of capital punishment are strong, tough, he-men, and those who are opposed to it are weak and unable to deal with the true question of human nature; that they are squeamish and soft. I disagree with that. I fought in a war; I saw death, bloodshed, carnage, savagery-all completely regrettable but which probably resulted in the winning of a war which, hopefully, permitted us to make improvements in our society. It also, of course, permitted us to make some regrettable mistakes.
I consider too that death is part of life, part of that long road of life that leads to the ultimate gate through which we all must pass. I think it is in that sense that we can approach this issue. It is not because we are adverse to the fact that people must be punished; not at all.
It seems to me that the return of capital punishment would be a retrograde step. It would have some effect in brutalizing segments of our society. I do not think there are compensatory factors which would make up for that.
On this issue as well as on others, what lies before us is the gigantic scale of decision. I suggest that if we place the weight of abolition on one side and all the evidence which we can glean from study, from speeches, and listening to other people, and if we can place on the other side the weight of those people who believe in the infliction of capital punishment, the scales would balance. If that be the case then it is not good enough for those who have come to that conclusion to simply say, "The general trend of opinion is moving toward hanging; the world is disturbed; there is more violence and, in spite of my doubt, I will go along with those who want the return of capital punishment." I believe that is wrong.
If the scales are evenly balanced it is essential to pour into the pan of abolition the invisible but heavy weight which says that society does not improve by deliberately killing anybody, and the onus must lie on those who say that one killing deserves another.
With all our sense of tragedy and sorrow for those who have been murdered, I doubt very much if they are standing in the next world demanding that we who are left here to organize our society are bound to dispatch their murderers by dropping them through a scaffold.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) for his remarks, many of which I subscribe to.
Even before we began our debate on this bill it was apparent to all of us that this is an issue that arouses a highly emotional response, by the members of this House and by those people whom we represent. Therefore I think it is especially important that we approach this issue with as dispassionate and rational an outlook as possible-without, however, ignoring the dictates of our conscience.
Those in favour of retaining the death penalty, or extending its application, argue that to abolish capital punishment is to show weakness toward the criminal element, to somehow reduce the protection of society, and
June 14, 1976

encourage the commission of crimes. I do not believe there is any justification for this view whatsoever.
First, it should be emphasized that there has been no proposal to remove the penal sanctions for the crime of murder, as some opponents of the bill have implied. The proposal in the bill is to replace capital punishment with a mandatory 25-year prison term, with severe restrictions on parole; this "life sentence" would in fact be the mandatory punishment for a greater number of crimes than are now punishable by death. I do not think this can be properly construed as a softening of attitude toward crime.
I think it can be shown conclusively that the death penalty is not an effective deterrent to murder, and that to view it as a solution to the problem of crime is extremely simplistic.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Let us see the figures.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Of all the offences, murder is most often committed in times of extreme emotional stress-during domestic quarrels, or in moments of panic during the commission of another crime. The deterrent effect of any punishment in such circumstances is negligible. This limitation of the deterrent theory of capital punishment was stated in a 1966 study done by the John Howard Association in Chicago. It said:
The kind of rationality assumed by the deterrent theory of capital punishment may be present in the minds of legislators at the time of their deliberations about crime and punishment and may even be present in the minds of most persons in their reflective moments. To attribute the qualitative thinking of a deliberative body to the participants in an emotional situation that leds to murder, however, is gross over-simplification of the psychological forces involved in homicides.
There is no more reason to assume the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent to the planned and deliberate murder. These crimes are most often committed by people with psychological abnormalities, who may not, however, fall within the legal definition of insanity. This type of personality is not deterred by the threat of remote punishment, no matter how severe, for some higher risks incurred by their behaviour may even increase the attraction to the crime being considered.
This is also true of the professional criminal, who merely accepts the risk of arrest and the prospect of punishment as part of the job. He is more likely to develop sophisticated techniques to avoid detection, that to be inhibited in his criminal conduct.
Experience in a number of countries bears out the theory of the ineffectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent. In the United States, for example, during the 15 year period from 1951 to 1966, the number of executions actually carried out in a year declined from 105 to one. During that period there was not significant change in the murder rate. When Denmark abolished the death penalty in 1933, the number of murders actually declined in the next few years.
Studies which compare American states retaining capital punishment with abolitionist states reveal that homicide rates follow the same trends in both groups; there is no difference in the number of killings that can be attributed to either the presence or the absence of the death penalty. Similarly, in states where the death penalty was reintroduced after a period of abolition, there was no significant
Capital Punishment
decrease in the number of murders. As Professor Sellin states:
If any conclusion can be drawn from all the above data, it is that there is no evidence that the abolition of the death penalty generally causes an increase in criminal homicides or that its reintroduction is followed by a decline. The explanation of changes in homicide rates must be sought elsewhere.
The death penalty has been shown, in numerous studies, to be no more effective than long prison terms in deterring crime; and if it is not an effective restraint then its retention cannot be justified.
It is essential that the state use no more force than is absolutely necessary to accomplish its appointed task when acting to protect the community from the commission of future crimes; when taking measures to rehabilitate criminals; or when inflicting punishment on those who have broken the law. This principle is inherent in our system of criminal justice; to depart from this principle and allow the legal system to administer excessively severe punishment is to undermine the values that the system is attempting to uphold. This view is supported by the Ontario Association of Professional Social Workers in a brief submitted to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). In calling for the total abolition of capital punishment the Association notes the failure of the death penalty to deter crime; it is, moreover, a weakening influence on our ethical and moral code since it reinforces the concept of the worthlessness of human life by an officially sanctioned violent act.
I might add that 15 years ago, at the University of Toronto School of Social Work I and Arthur Martin, who then was one of the most eminent counsel in Canada and now has been elevated to the Ontario Court of Appeal, participated in a debate on capital punishment. I spoke as an abolitionist. Two eminent counsel opposed us. I have never changed my mind.
A special commission established in Massachusetts to investigate the question of capital punishment reached the same conclusion, namely:
The existence of capital punishment tends to cheapen human life. It tends to encourage both children and adults to believe that physical violence, the ultimate form of which is putting an individual to death, is a proper method of solving social and personal conflict... The only moral ground on which the state could conceivably possess the right to destroy human life would be if this were indispensable for the protection or preservation of other lives. This places the burden of proof on those who believe that capital punishment exercises a deterrent effect on the potential criminal. Unless they can establish that the death penalty does, in fact, protect other lives, at the expense of one, there is no moral justification for the state to 'take life'.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the death penalty can be shown as protecting lives; I do not believe that its retention can be morally justified. We have a duty to protect society from the criminal; we must punish, and we must use all the methods within our competence to rehabilitate. But we must not seek revenge for an act already committed; revenge neither restores the victim nor expiates the crime.
Opposition to the abolition of capital punishment has been expressed by some of our police forces. While they have a legitimate concern for their own safety, I do not think the death penalty would reduce the hazards of their

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
job. It not only fails to deter, but also creates an added risk. The criminal facing certain execution has nothing to lose by taking advantage of any means possible either to avoid detention or escape from custody. Prison guards and police officers would therefore be in even greater danger during the inevitable lapse of time before the death penalty could be carried out. The task of law enforcement can be made less dangerous only by reducing the level of violence in our society, and imposing capital punishment has precisely the opposite effect.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would refer to the emphasis that has been placed in the course of debate on this bill on the increasing crime rate, particularly the rapid rise in recent years in the number of murders. Certainly we must not ignore the social context in which this bill has been introduced. It is imperative that the government proceed with a co-ordinated and comprehensive program to attempt to reverse this trend of increasing lawlessness. We have had an undertaking by the minister that prison facilities will be made more secure. Revisions of the Criminal Code and the abolition of all unearned remissions of sentence have already been proposed to the House. This type of effort, combined with thorough study and extensive social programs that attack the root causes of crime are, in the long run, the only means of ensuring the safety of our law-abiding citizens. The hanging of a handful of criminals will do nothing to further the attainment of that goal of security.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, more than anything else, this debate has shown how thick is the skin of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) when an abolitionist speaks and how thin it is when a retention-ist speaks.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Here we go again!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hon. members are making personal arguments. Discuss the issue, not the man.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many instances we rely on the information which is made available by a minister responsible for a bill. Although the minister spoke of engaging people who have looked into the matter of retention, to the best of my knowledge none of that literature has been delivered to my desk. I checked again today. Therefore if the minister's skin is somewhat thin, he has himself to blame.
I have a great deal of respect for the opinions of some individuals and am disappointed at not being able to support the position of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), for whom I have the greatest respect. As a man, he is most persuasive.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: And very sensible.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: That is a matter of measurement. The hon. member may have prejudged, instead of keeping an open mind.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: He adopted an enlightened position.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no member takes lightly his responsibility for voting on this bill. Each member will vote only after he has given the matter a great deal of

thought and consideration. After all, each one of us must decide, as democratically elected members of this House, how best we can preserve the safety of the individual in society, how best to preserve law and order so that people feel safe. If any hon. member is of the opinion that the interests of law and order are better served with the retention of capital punishment, then, no matter what his conscience may tell him in some respect, he is obligated to opt for capital punishment. That is the situation we face.
I agree that in many instances capital punishment probably will not deter a person from taking the life of a fellow citizen. For instance, I am convinced that it will not normally deter the individual who quarrels at a party or quarrels at home, and is irritated to the point of reacting in such a fashion that he takes the life of an individual. No, there is no way by which a law of man can deter such an act on the part of a fellow man. But I am convinced that we must bring law to the land.
As long as I knew I would probably get a concurrent sentence, as has been given in our courts too often, in the course of a robbery I would probably be quite prepared to take a life if it meant I could escape undetected and free. Any individual may be prepared to rob a bank and brandish a gun, but is he prepared to face capital punishment as a consequence of that act? At that point in time it has to deter the individual from a course of action which might bring him a consecutive sentence rather than a concurrent sentence, or which might give him capital punishment as a reward.
When an individual is incarcerated for an extended period of time, he probably has little if anything to lose if he is going to get a concurrent sentence for a further crime within the institution in which he is confined. However, I doubt very much if he will put his life on the line by taking the life of another individual while in that institution. In that instance he would at least have cause for thought, and it probably would be a deterrent to that individual.
We have come through a cycle in which law and order were preached, taught, respected and understood. The periods of time which have been cited as examples for the reason why we should abolish capital punishment are in an era in the thirties, and come forward to the forties and fifties. Let us briefly go back to that period of time and look at the type of law and order which we had.
The Queen of England and her husband visited Canada in 1939. She rode in an open touring car or convertible, with the top down when the weather would permit. When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister of this country, as well as when Mr. Pearson and Mr. St. Laurent were Prime Minister, they rode in ordinary cars bought on the street which they purchased themselves. They did not have bullet proof glass or armour plate.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: They had it for the Queen.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
They did not have it for the Queen on either of the two visits I mentioned. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has two automobiles, both of which are armour-plated and both of which have bullet proof glass. That is very symbolic of the level to which law
June 14, 1976

and order have sunk. It is time we began to appraise when a man has lost his right to live in the society of his fellowmen. We have to think of that in terms of the good of all society.
I could not possibly vote for this bill for the same reason that the right hon. member for Prince Albert could not vote for it. In an act of treason, an individual or group of individuals who commit that act are not necessarily acting against the life of an individual. They are acting against a multitude, which is the state, and they are prepared to endanger that multitude regardless of what may be the consequence to the perpetrator of the deed. That is a heinous crime indeed. It should and must remain on the statutes of Canada.
Let us move to other types of crime. What about the individual who was putting bombs in mail boxes, mailing bombs through the mail, placing bombs in public places, endangering, and in some cases succeeding in taking the lives of innocent people? That man, representing his own personal position which is not the position of society as a whole, has sacrificed his right to live in society. Society will only be safe when he is no longer among us. We are responsible to society to make decisions which may be hard to come by in our consciences but which are in the best interests of the total good.
What about the individual who, for personal or philosophical reasons, chooses to try to hijack an airplane and endangers the lives of scores of people? Should that man or woman be given the right to continue life among us? I submit that society is looking for the punishment which may deter the act of such an individual. That is what society is at least hoping for.
What about the contract killer? He is present among us whether we like it or not. Whether the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice dismiss this man in any way, shape or form, he is among us in Canada. He is for hire, for the objective of the individual who hires him at a varying price which is reputed in some cases to be quite low indeed for the removal of an insignificant individual. Yet that man may have made his living for quite some time by removing people from among our numbers. A perpetrator of a deed like that who is willing to do the same deed again has sacrificed his right to live in society.
I am not one who wishes to dangle the noose nor do I associate capital punishment with the noose. I believe we can at least extend a more civilized means of extermination. I am sorry there is no better word to use. However, I do not associate it with the noose nor would I want to see the noose used if we do have capital punishment.
We have reports from those working in the psychiatric field. None of those people are prepared to give at any point in time a qualified yes or no as to whether an individual has been rehabilitated. It does not mean that because an individual has been in jail under the best of instruction, guidance, and treatment for up to 25 years, he will change his way of life. Nor does it mean that his psychology has reached the norm which can be expected and respected by the psychiatric profession.
We are dealing with something to which statistics do not apply. We are dealing with the erratic behaviour of an individual who is not normal or he would never have
Capital Punishment
committed the crime about which we are talking. That is the individual over whom we have no control, or any measurement or capability of predicting his future.
I am concerned about one thing. I would appreciate it if at some point in time the Solicitor General would give us the date and the name of the individual who corrected the position he outlined in this House in respect of this bill. I am not arguing with him, but I would like to have the reference. If the government were to disrespect one last tradition, and it has disrespected many that relate to democracy as we know it, and had tradition been the guideline of government, there are cabinet ministers who would not be holding that position today. They disrespect tradition. But the Solicitor General advises us that the cabinet will have to vote with the government because the bill was introduced by a cabinet minister and is a government bill.
I submit that regardless of the rank or position of anyone in this party, there has been absolutely no pressure to vote any way as far as any Conservative has been concerned since I have been associated with this bill. The same cannot be said of those to your right, Mr. Speaker. It might be traditional that when a government bill is introduced all cabinet members vote for it, but on the basis of the past behaviour of the government this tradition should not be any problem in connection with the bill before us. I hope the vote will be free.

speechtext: That is not a point of order. It is a point of stupidity.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I am expressing an opinion of my own, but one which I hope is shared by others.
I have been elected only on two occasions, not for many years as have other members of the House. My position is well known in my constituency. I have answered every letter I received on this subject, whether from my constituency or from elsewhere. I have expressed my opinions as I am expressing them tonight. I have expressed them to church organizations which favour abolition, I have expressed them to individuals who favour retention.
I have said to public meetings in my constituency that I favour the retention of capital punishment, though not clear down the line, as used to be the situation 20, 30 or 50 years ago. I do favour it for those crimes of murder which symbolize to society that citizens are not as safe as they should be, and for crimes which involve the lives of more than one person. Society deserves this protection from the House, and it is our responsibility to provide it.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has been hanging around the House for a long time now.

June 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
Everyone who has spoken, everyone I have heard, has been sincere in his comments and has given reasons for being prepared to vote one way or the other.
We have heard all kinds of statistics. One thing we learned from that, if nothing else, is that you can always find statistics to prove whatever point you wish to make. The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), a friend of mine for whom I have a great deal of respect, quoted statistics which clearly show that the murder rate in countries where abolition is in force is lower than it is in countries where retention is the law. I have some other figures. They come from a book which was prepared for the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) himself, at his request, and they show the opposite. They compare France, a retentionist country, with three other countries. I wanted to put these figures on the record because it seems logical to balance the information given.
In France, the murder rate is 3.28 per hundred thousand compared with the rate in Germany of 4 per hundred thousand. The rate in Austria, an abolitionist country, is a little lower. A similar rate prevails in Norway. But in the case of Germany, an abolitionist country, the murder rate is indeed higher. What this proves is that it is impossible for us, in the context of our own country, to use figures from other countries around the world to determine what effect either abolition or retention might have on the murder rate here.
We have conflicting reports regarding the efficacy of capital punishment in reducing murder rates. In the case of our own country, virtual abolition has resulted in a substantially higher rate. Look at the figures from 1940 to 1959. The murder rate was almost constant at about 1.2 per 100,000. Since 1959 it has risen to 2.4. we also know that the last hanging which took place in this country was in the early sixties and that since then there has been an increase in the murder rate amounting to 150 per cent. I do not believe any statistician will argue that this is not a significant increase.
I want to suggest something new. One of the criticisms made by members on the government side who want this debate to end quickly is that little which is new has been said-that no new proposals are being made. The proposal I wish to make is not new in terms of being an original idea, but it is new in terms of this bill. At least I have not heard it expressed in the debate so far.
If we are research-oriented and believe that through scientific research we can come up with the best answers to problems facing our country, we should be thinking of another five-year period of research. We have gone through eight years of abolition by law and a lot more than that, perhaps 15 years, of de facto abolition by commutation. The result has been a 150 per cent increase in the murder rate. We must now decide whether to abolish capital punishment or to retain it. The best thing to do, I suggest, is to try another five-year period of enforcement of the death penalty. It seems to me that if we do this, and if the murder rate goes down, it can be taken as evidence that capital punishment is indeed a deterrent to murder. But if the murder rate continues to go up we would know there is not necessarily any kind of relationship.
To some this might appear to be a strange suggestion. But I do not think it is possible to determine the effect of
(Mr. Yewchuk.l
capital punishment in our own national context in any other way, for example, by comparing the situation here with the situation in European countries or in Africa or anywhere else in the world. I do not think their figures are necessarily significant in this context since other countries are different in many ways. Their social conditions, laws, attitudes, religion, culture, way of life and their problems are different, so I suggest we cannot really compare ourselves with other countries because it is something like comparing apples and oranges. Even social conditions in Canada change from one year to the next, but if we could find the closest possible similarity in some kind of experimental setting then I would think it would be worth considering. Perhaps an amendment of this kind could be made to the bill, which I suggest would make it a little simpler to deal with.
One of the most compelling arguments against capital punishment, I think, is the possibility that an innocent person might be hanged. I do not think anyone would argue against that possibility. Nevertheless we must consider the other side of the coin, which is the possibility that a convicted murderer might kill again. According to the figures that I have been able to obtain from the best source available to me-indeed I obtained this information more by rumour-there has been one innocent person who was hanged in this country, and this took place some 30 or 40 years ago. On the other hand, figures from Statistics Canada show that since 1963 there have been seven repeat murders. Seven other innocent victims have been murdered by people who had been found guilty of murder and then paroled or released from prison having served their sentence. Or perhaps the second murder took place while they were still in custody. That is another statistic that should be considered. Weighing the possibility of a repeat murder occurring against that of hanging an innocent person, the chance of a repeat murder occurring is seven times greater. I think that figure speaks in favour of capital punishment for convicted murderers.
Some people have suggested that capital punishment might be used for other than the traditionally accepted reason. I am thinking here of people who are involved in the illicit drug trade, such as heroin suppliers and distributors. We often hear of heroin addicts dying from an overdose of heroin and I wonder how often these overdoses are accidental. It seems to me that if someone involved in the importation or distribution of heroin thinks that a user could report him to the police, there would be no simpler way of disposing of that user than by supplying him with a much stronger dose which the user would inject and thus kill himself. Perhaps the bill should be broadened to include such possibilities as this.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, the real issue here is not necessarily whether capital punishment is a deterrent or is not a deterrent. Rather the real issue revolves around our responsibility as the elected representatives of the people. As all hon. members will admit, we have a responsibility in this House to speak on behalf of those who sent us here. This is why we have representative government. Our whole democratic system is based on the principle that we are elected to this place for the prime purpose of speaking out on behalf of those who sent us here.
June 14, 1976

According to surveys that have been made, about 80 per cent of the people of this country feel that capital punishment should be retained at this time. If members of parliament choose to ignore this supposed will of the people, then we have to ask ourselves whether representative government, or democracy, is indeed functioning at all. If we take it upon ourselves to go against the will of the people, we being the representatives of the people, then we are behaving in no better fashion than as an autocratic dictator imposing our will upon the people, telling them what is good for them rather than reflecting their views in this House.
I am not trying to belittle the importance of the conscience of an individual member; that is a most important consideration as well. On the other hand we must keep in mind our responsibility to those who elected us. A lot of people in Canada feel that revenge is not necessarily all bad, that the principle of an eye for an eye is not necessarily all bad. As a matter of fact a lot of people think it is a good idea. I am not expressing my own personal view, but it is something that must be kept in mind.
Much has been said about rehabilitation of murderers. I am informed by my statistical source that the rate of rehabilitation has been rather good; that less than one per cent of homicidal offenders who were paroled in the U.S. have been returned to prison because they committed another murder. However, a larger percentage is returned for other reasons. Even though we know that some murderers cannot be rehabilitated, the figures point to the fact that most of them do not murder again.
There have also been comments about the cost of keeping men in prison for 25 years. This bill proposes to keep people convicted of murder in prison for 25 years. I am informed that the cost of keeping a person incarcerated is approximately $18,000 a year. Multiplied by 25, that works out at about half a million dollars per prisoner, in terms of 1976 constant dollars. We must ask ourselves whether a taxpayer who has already suffered because someone close to him or someone he may have known-an innocent person-has been murdered, should be asked on top of that to spend another $500,000 to keep the convicted murderer in jail for 25 years. It seems to me that that is a rather expensive proposition.
I was interested in the comment the other day of the whip on the other side. The governing party takes the position when talking in public that there is going to be a free vote on this bill, although we know that there is not really going to be a free vote at all. The other day the government whip stood up in the House and proudly announced that he was a retentionist. Then in the very next breath, the next sentence, he said, "Let's hurry up and get this bill passed". I wonder just how much of a retentionist he can be when he wants to pass a bill to abolish capital punishment. That is the kind of consistency we have seen from him ever since he has been a member of parliament.
