speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: One way or the other.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the whip clarify his position, because he still looks fuzzy in his position over there, and I am afraid that does not help clarify how he really feels about it. I only have a few minutes left until ten o'clock and I am not sure what time I started, but I do want to put on the record some other reasons why capital punishment is perhaps a good idea, and these are some of the reasons accepted by the United Nations.
One reason is that capital punishment represents a political necessity for the protection not merely of society but of the social order itself. Another is that if the state is to be denied the right to take the life of one of its members, then by the same token it should be denied the right to deprive that member in perpetuity of his liberty. In other words, if the state does not have the right to hang somebody, does the state have the right to put him in jail for 25 years? That is a question I have not heard answered in this place.
I think the key argument that should be stressed here is that capital punishment is a just and appropriate one in so far as murder is concerned. Perhaps above all other punishments it marks society's detestation and abhorrence of the taking of life and its revulsion against the crime of crimes. Capital punishment is required in the case of a subsequent murder in prison or in the course of escape by a convicted murderer, because if this existing deterrent were removed, apprehension would exist concerning the safety of the prison staff and the general public from prisoners for whom, because they are already serving life sentences, a further sentence of imprisonment could have no deterrent effect. In other words, if a man were serving a life sentence for murder and he knew he could not be hanged for another murder, why not murder again in an attempt to get away? This is a fairly compelling argument in favour of capital punishment.
There is also the argument that capital punishment is a painless and more humane form of treatment for a murderer than life imprisonment. Life imprisonment, it is argued, is more cruel, but that is a matter of opinion, of course.
The punishment inflicted for a grave crime should adequately reflect the revulsion felt by the great majority of citizens, and the ultimate justification of any punishment is not that it is a deterrent but that it is the emphatic denunciation by the community of a crime, and from this point of view there are some murders which demand the most emphatic denunciation of all, namely, the death penalty.
It is reasonable to suppose that the deterrent force of capital punishment operates not only by affecting the conscious thoughts of individuals tempted to commit murder, but also by building up in the community over a long period of time a deep feeling of peculiar abhorrence for the crime of murder.
Where murder is premeditated it is only common sense to assume that not only the chances of detection but also the consequences in the vent of detection are ordinarily taken into consideration. The death penalty may be the

June 14, 1976
Adjournment Debate
only effective deterrent against a life prisoner making a murderous assault on a fellow prisoner or member of the prison staff.
Statistics, which ordinarily fail to demonstrate the deterrent effect of capital punishment, are for the most part assembled by those who wish to abolish the death penalty. In other words, such statistics are not compiled on the way to reaching a conclusion but, rather to support a conclusion already reached morally, philosophically or intuitively. Statistics are susceptible to different interpretations, and are unreliable and misleading. It is almost impossible to draw valid comparisons between different countries owing to differences in the legal definition of crimes, the practice of the prosecuting authorities and the courts, methods of compiling criminal statistics, moral standards, customary behaviour, and political, social, and economical conditions.
Upon the view that the deterrent effect of capital punishment resides primarily in its long-term effect on the attitude of society to murder, it is not to be expected that variations in the number of executions from year to year would be directly reflected in a rise or fall in the murder rate. A negative conclusion to be drawn from statistics does not imply a conclusion that the deterrent effect of the death penalty is not greater than that of any other punishment. It means only that the figures afford no reliable evidence one way or the other. It would be equally difficult to show statistically a direct relationship between the severity of any other punishment and the incidence of the crime to which it relates.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, for those who are in the habit of pointing out the countries where the murder rate has dropped after the death penalty has been abolished, those statistics do not in any way imply that the murder rate would not have dropped even more had it been retained.
There are many ways that we must look at these statistics to be sure we do not get fooled by them because, as I said at the beginning of my comments, anyone can find statistics to prove the conclusion he has already reached. We have seen many examples of that in this debate, rather than looking at the statistics and trying to conclude something from them. Mr. Speaker, may I now call it ten o'clock and conclude my remarks on another occasion?
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF IMMIGRANTS- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENSURE ADEQUACY
IMMIGRATION-MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF IMMIGRANTS- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENSURE ADEQUACY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am again referring to a question I asked the minister on May 19 as recorded at page 13663 of Hansard. This relates to a comparatively new exotic disease in Canada, and the ques-

tion was asked with that in mind. I want to use the city of Toronto as an example to lay the groundwork for this matter.
It has been estimated there are about 10,000 in that area living underground, sharing living quarters with people who conceal their presence from officials. This, of course, causes a drain in taxes to the legitimate taxpayer in the area. These people living thus are denied the basic social services and even the protection of the law. They are vulnerable to unscrupulous employers and are paid below the minimum wage. Their fear of being exposed makes them more vulnerable, leaving them open to further exploitation.
These people can become a public health problem as many of them are harbouring parasites common in their country of origin and they have had no adequate treatment. In the field of pediatrics it is becoming more and more apparent that, due to the multiracial society in which we live, and this is very true in a city like Toronto, we are developing a considerable range of tropical and sub-tropical diseases. These diseases are imported not only by immigrants but even by travellers who have visited tropical countries.
Many times doctors who look at them have had no experience in the treatment of tropical medicine. Therefore a doctor often misses the diagnosis, forgetting even the geographic area from which the patients came. The question for the tourist is, where have you been and when?
This incidence in the increase of such diseases is particularly true in the city of Toronto where over half the old downtown area is composed of immigrants, many of whom cannot speak English. Certainly the majority of their children of pre-school age cannot do so. These people often have been let into the country with a health certificate which states that they have been examined in their own country. Such an examination could have been carried out six months before the person left the country and such a person could have become infected in the meantime. The possibilities are there. In any event the measure of capability of these countries to find and pick up infection is not of the same high standard as practised in the western world. In other words, patients can get a certificate stating that they are free of parasites only to find here in Canada that they are infested with parasites.
We need immigrants in Canada; there is no question about that. We are all immigrants. Certainly immigrants have done work Canadians would not do, and they have done it willingly. However, an added strain is placed on the immigrant when he is accused of harbouring tropical diseases such as intestinal parasites.
I should like to congratulate the minister for the proposals he announced today of a new control mechanism for the issuance of social insurance numbers. I think this is a good move. Visitors to Canada who wish to obtain work will have a distinctive number nine as the first digit in their social insurance card. I suggest that the minister should provide that these people be given another number to go with the new social insurance number, with which they would be able to go to a clinic, be examined, and be declared free of intestinal parasites. This would save thou-
June 14, 1976

sands and thousands of dollars and would spare the immigrant and his family the humiliation of harbouring parasitic disease. This, I feel, is how the problem could be solved.
It would be ideal of course if this work could be done in the country of origin just before the immigrant comes to Canada, especially if it were done in such a way that we could depend on the validity of the certificate which would be rendered stating that the person is free of infection. But as I have stated before, this is almost an impossibility.
All these people should be insured under our medicare plan. This also includes foreign students. Often these people are afraid to go to a doctor and tell him of their illness because of the fear of going to hospital and having their illness exposed. Certainly is is up to the Department of Immigration to see that these people, upon application for a social insurance number, also are required to have an examination and that the information is indicated on the card stating that they have been examined and are free of disease. If there is parasitic disease, this then could be followed up by physicians who are trained in the treatment of these infections.
Because of large scale immigration from tropical and sub-tropical countries, where standards of sanitation are much lower or non-existent, we have been flooded with infestation rarely seen before. Only recently has the Department of Immigration made it mandatory to have stool cultures done on applicants from certain countries. Anyone infested is a potential carrier and contaminator of others such as family, friends, and so on. Worms and parasites are passed on due to poor hygiene. Most parasites are found all over the world, and the precentage of any population harbouring them is determined by public health standards, living conditions, and so on.
Toronto's main parasitology clinic is at the Toronto General Hospital. It is certainly one of the biggest in Canada. But the clinic is able to treat only about 1,500 cases a year. It is inadequately funded, and its waiting lists are far too long. More personnel must be recruited and trained in tropical medicine so that cases can be seen, speedily treated, and handled. That would save a lot of money. Sufficient funding is needed to do this necessary work. Let us not be penny wise and pound foolish as we are at the present time. I suggest to the minister that he can now take a little more glory for himself for putting the number nine on isurance cards. Let him put another number on to be sure that this work I have mentioned is fully carried out.

speakeroldname: Mr. Arthur Portelance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF IMMIGRANTS- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENSURE ADEQUACY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) raised the matter regarding the medical examination of immigrants the minister gave a brief account of the situation and pointed out that other efforts were being made in this area.
Any immigrant seeking admission to Canada must undergo a medical examination pursuant to the provisions of the Immigration Act, and before he leaves his native country he is judged on the basis of the universal standards as set by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Adjournment Debate
Because of the number of non-immigrants, some 40 million, who enter Canada each year it is impossible, considering the expenses that practice would entail, and inappropriate, considering our desire to facilitate the admission of visitors, to have everyone of them undergo medical examination. So our policy is to have a medical examination for people most likely to present a risk to public health. It is estimated that the degree of risk increases with the duration of the stay and the nature of the activities of that person while he on she remains in Canada. All non-immigrants who plan on staying a year or more must undergo a medical examination and so do people who intend to take up a job in certain fields such as food preparation, the hotel business, hospital care, and so on. In addition, in cooperation with the Department of National Health and Welfare the department for which he is responsible intends to have other groups of non-immigrants undergo a medical examination when they are likely to present a risk to public health.
In addition, an increasing number of Canadians take holidays or a job for a prolonged period in certain countries where certain diseases exist. When they return to Canada they are granted admission as of right and they do not have to take a medical examination. That explains at least in part the emergence of certain diseases in Canada.
I would like to reassure the hon. member that the department of which the minister is in charge, in cooperation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, is doing its best to ensure that the Canadian public is not exposed to parasitic or other diseases.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-PROPOSED CLOSING OF RCA LABORATORIES IN MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
INDUSTRY-PROPOSED CLOSING OF RCA LABORATORIES IN MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, On May 28 I asked the following question of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson):
Is the minister yet in a position to report to the House as to whether the government has been able to prevent the RCA research laboratories in Montreal from closing at the direction of the RCA head office in the United States? Inasmuch as such a closing would clash directly with the principles of international business conduct which when tabled in the House last July were stated as reflecting government policy, could the minister tell us whether the government will take steps to make a reasonable degree of compliance with these principles mandatory and to fully monitor the extent of such compliance on the part of all foreign-controlled enterprises in Canada, the firms to which the government has said these principles apply?
The minister replied in part:
What action we may be able to take in law or what kind of enforcement measures we may be able to undertake are questions I am considering at the present time. But I am at present carrying on talks with the RCA company in an effort to see whether they can be persuaded to change the policy. The second part of the question was somewhat more complex than I could follow, since it was related to the RCA issue. Perhaps my hon. friend would wish to ask a supplementary.
Since it is evident to hon. members that government members are rarely, if ever, recognized during the question period to ask supplementary questions, I asked that this question be set down for the adjournment debate to give the minister a chance to respond to the second part of my question.

June 14, 1976
Adjournment Debate
As I pointed out, last July 18, 1975, the then minister of industry, trade and commerce tabled in this House a new set of guiding principles for good corporate behaviour. In the statement he made at that time he said in part:
Like the earlier set of "Guiding Principles of Good Corporate Behaviour", the new set of principles reflects broad government policy regarding the activities and responsibilities of foreign-controlled business enterprises in Canada. They thus provide an added indication of the sort of benefits the government looks for in assessing investment proposals under the Foreign Investment Review Act. But they are directed toward all foreign controlled enterprises doing business in Canada, whether they are involved with the Foreign Investment Review Act or not.
It seems to me that the recent decision of the head office of RCA in the United States to close its Canadian research laboratories in Montreal clearly clashes with these principles. Let me point to three of them in particular. Principle one says that foreign-controlled firms in Canada should:
Pursue a high degree of autonomy in the exercise of decision-making and risk-taking functions, including innovative activity and the marketing of any resulting new products.
Principle two says that foreign-controlled firms in Canada should:
Develop as an integral part of the Canadian operation an autonomous capability for technological innovation, including research, development, engineering, industrial design and preproduction activities; and for production, marketing, purchasing and accounting.
Principle four states that foreign-controlled firms in Canada should:
Strive for a full international mandate for innovation and market development, when it will enable the Canadian company to improve its efficiency by specialization of productive operations.
At this laboratory a team had been built up of some 62 highly-qualified research scientists and engineers. The press has reported that the closing of this laboratory will mean that only 16 of this group will be found other jobs in RCA plants in Canada. The other 42, according to the press report may-not necessarily will but may-be found jobs not in Canada but in plants or laboratories in the United States operated by the U.S. parent company.
This Canadian research facility is being closed not because the Canadian company is in difficulty, not because the laboratory is not productive. It is being done because of the management difficulties of the world-wide RCA interests and the resulting efforts of the new head office management of RCA to deal with the situation created during the term of its predecessor.
It is time to ask again what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has been able to achieve in his discussions with RCA to get that company to change its decision to close the laboratory, on a voluntary basis. If this decision has not been reversed-and for that matter even if it has been-this situation shows the importance of making these guidelines mandatory in the sense I outlined in my question.
The company claims it is adhering to the guidelines but I say what it is doing appears to clash with the definite words of the guidelines. I challenge the president of the company to show how it will meet the guidelines if the laboratory is closed and research work, to whatever extent it is carried on, is continued only in divisions of the

company in Canada. The guidelines are government policy, but the government has no way of ensuring that foreign-controlled companies comply with them. The company claims it does not need the laboratory because the climate is not right due to the government's increasing intervention in the economic system.
RCA did not class it as excessive intervention when it accepted $20 million from the government-then it was not excessive or undue interference.
Industrial research and development in Canada are not increasing. They have declined as a percentage of the Gross National Product. The government needs new programs to stimulate this, and part of its efforts must be to deal with the situation created where decisions are made by foreign-controlled firms with the head office following world-wide priorities which clash with Canadian priorities in spite of the viability and economic strength of the Canadian operations in question.
To conclude, the government must act promptly not only to correct the RCA case but also to ensure that it is not the first of similar, unwarranted decisions taken by other foreign controlled firms in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-PROPOSED CLOSING OF RCA LABORATORIES IN MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the hon. member for having raised this situation which is the subject of much discussion and concern on the part of some hon. members, especially those from the Montreal area.
It is true that the company has recently announced in a brief press release its reorganization plan in Canada. The minister discussed this with the chairman and the chief executive of the company and particularly tried to find out how this project would affect the present research activities of the company. We have learned that this decision would be reflected in fact by reductions of the research and development expenses of RCA in Canada and that this must be considered in the following context: First, the major part of the yearly sales of the company come from two main sources, that is the manufacture of television sets, including picture tubes, and the division of electronic systems for the government and private companies, that I shall simply call the space division. This division manufactures microwave material, transponders for satellites and satellite ground stations. The research and development work for the manufacture of television sets has never been pushed very much in Canada. Most of the research of RCA Limited has always been aimed at its space division.
In 1974, the work accomplished until that time in the various commercial divisions was regrouped in a single research laboratory. This laboratory continued to serve commercial divisions, but it also got involved in more and more projects bearing no relation with the industrial activities of RCA. The result of the recent decision to centralize research facilities will be that all research for commercial divisions will be done in each division. Only the research elements having no relation with the industrial activities of the company will be relinquished.
The company has assured the minister that this will not affect at all its present production commitments, which insurance seems to us particularly important for the space
June 14, 1976

division. This division is the only one to produce for the parent company transponders that go into the manufacture of all the commercial satellites that it sells in the United States and elsewhere. The division also holds sales rights throughout the world for all the products that it manufactures and it has in fact sold abroad much of its telecommunication and satellite ground station material. It is therefore inaccurate to say that RCA will stop its research activities. But it is true that it will pursue in the future only those which can meet the needs of its various divisions.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to make a few remarks on some of the government legislation designed to ensure respect for international principles in matters of trade ethics, namely that the problem of obtaining reports based on those guiding principles are now being actively studied in the more general context of trade relations. The government is concerned about reducing as much as possible the burden of reports the Canadian businesses have to fill out. On the other hand, we must see to it that enough pertinent data is placed at the disposal of the government and the private sector to allow for formulation of a reasonable and realist policy. It is very difficult to conciliate those most desirable objectives, but I trust it will be possible to lighten the present burden of reports while, at the same time, obtaining enough information to allow control over the type of conduct mentioned by my hon. colleague.

subtopic: PUBLICATIONS-POSSIBILITY OF ACTION TO CONTROL DISTRIBUTION OF MAGAZINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
PUBLICATIONS-POSSIBILITY OF ACTION TO CONTROL DISTRIBUTION OF MAGAZINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 1 as reported at page 14027 of Hansard, I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) the following question:
. . . The minister has frequently expressed concern about foreign domination of the film distribution industry in Canada and has in fact encouraged provincial departments to initiate legislation in this area. I would like to ask the minister whether he has worked with the same intensity to bring magazine distribution under domestic control and in a way which would limit exploitation of sex and the almost unabated flow of pornography into this country.
The Minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I would approach that with the same degree of zest.
I would applaud any effort on the part of the minister to repatriate Canadian dollars which would otherwise flow to another country. If he can also do something of benefit for the film distribution industry in that regard, I would applaud him for that action too. But I am discouraged. Although the minister takes initiatives to help the domestic part of the film distribution industry, which is outside his jurisdiction and, essentially, under provincial jurisdiction, he does not show the same concern for the distribution of magazines in our country.
It is good to promote independence, Mr. Speaker. But that kind of independence he is promoting is lopsided. On one hand he will eliminate Time magazine because he thinks it is a shame that any of our Canadian dollars should go south of the border to United States. I again underscore the fact that I would like to see those dollars remain in Canada.
Adjournment Debate
He is making a very dismal choice. He is encouraging the decline and the demise of Time magainze. At the same time he is not doing anything to discourage the inflow of magazines such as Penthouse, Playboy, Hustler and other pornography. The minister says he does not have the same kind of zest for stemming the flow of that kind of product into the country.
It seems a little bit inconsistent that we spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on caps for medicine bottles so that children cannot open them and destroy themselves. We spend thousands of dollars advertising on behalf of household safety with regard to medicines, fire, and swimming pools. However, here we have a major pollutant which destroys the perception and expectations of children, and which is much more readily available than patent medicines. In its own way it is just as destructive, yet the minister says he does not have the same zest for steaming that tide.
This self-appointed, self-proclaimed prophet of Canadian culture, the Secretary of State, becomes very concerned when Canadian dollars go south into the bank account of Time Incorporated. However, he does not mind if by way of American distribution companies Canadian dollars flow south into the bank accounts of gangster organizations.
I have before me a page from the Toronto Star, dated Saturday, May 22. The headline reads: "Maclean's Brass Charged Over Skin Magazines". I remember when we were dealing with Bill C-58, the chairman of the board and the president of Maclean's magazine appeared before the committee. Oh, the saccharine piety those two men spewed out about the great Canadian culture that we have. They referred to Birks, Hudson's Bay, and all the other great symbols of Canadian culture-and all the time they were promoting a distribution company in the city of Toronto of which the main profit was derived from the distribution of pornography. What kind of hypocrisy is that?
The minister, the self-proclaimed self-appointed cultural czar of Canada, was really up tight to make sure that Time got out of Canada. He also wanted to get rid of Reader's Digest. However, he says he does not have the same kind of zest for getting rid of pornographic magazines.
You can go to any magazine shop in the country. The display of magazines will be somewhat in this order. On the very top shelf, almost out of reach of even adults, are magazines like Field and Stream, Better Homes and Gardens, and other such magazines. On the bottom shelf, six inches off the floor where all the little kids can get at them, you find Oui, Penthouse, Playboy, Hustler and all those other magazines. However, the minister says he does not have the same kind of zest for stemming the flow of that kind of literature into Canada.
It is discouraging when a minister of the Crown has a great concern about a few tax dollars going south of the border, but no concern about the mental, spiritual, and emotional health of kids when they read this kind of pornography. This minister should re-evaluate and reorder his priorities and perspective to be sure he serves the Canadian people well by preserving the mental and spiritual health of our young people.

June 14, 1976

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PUBLICATIONS-POSSIBILITY OF ACTION TO CONTROL DISTRIBUTION OF MAGAZINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in response to the hon. member on behalf of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Miss Campbell), who is absent on official duty.
With respect to the question raised by the hon. member I should like to emphasize that there are now 16 distributors in Canada operating on a national scale. Of these, four are wholly Canadian-owned, 25 per cent. Rather than contemplating the restriction of the activities of the foreign-owned operators, the government is focusing on a more positive approach, namely, the improvement of the promotional and distribution capabilities of Canadian-owned
publishers and distributors. The Canada Council administers a $1.5 million program annually to this end.
There is no intention to curtail the entry into Canada of foreign magazines above and beyond certain tariff regulations. For instance, item 99221 restricts the entry into Canada of periodicals, postcards, inserts or coupons printed outside Canada and containing 5 per cent or more advertising aimed at the domestic Canadian market.
On a second point, it should be noted that tariff item 99201/1 already prohibits the entry into Canada of "books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations-of a treasonable or seditious or of an immoral or indecent character." The application of the Criminal Code to the dissemination of such material falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
